title: Absolute convergence
text: Definitions \sum a_n is absolutely convergent if \sum|a_n|<\infty. It is conditionally convergent if it converges but \sum|a_n|=\infty. Theorem (real or complex series) Absolute convergence \implies convergence. Proof: \left|\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}a_k\right|\le\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}|a_k|\longrightarrow0 \quad\text{uniformly for }mn\to\infty. Apply Cauchy criterion for series. Converse fails: \sum(-1)^n/n converges by Alternating Series Test, while \sum1/n diverges. Rearrangements: absolute convergence preserves the sum under every rearrangement. For a conditionally convergent real series, a rearrangement can change the sum or make it diverge; it need not do so for every rearrangement. Links: Partial sums · Comparison test · Alternating Series Test · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 9

title: Adjoint
text: Let V,W be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces over \mathbb R or \mathbb C, and let T:V\to W be linear. Adjoint The unique linear map T^:W\to V satisfying \langle Tx,y\rangle_W=\langle x,T^y\rangle_V\quad(x\in V,\ y\in W) is the adjoint of T. Existence follows by representing the functional x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle for each y; see Dual space. Rules (with compatible domains): (S+T)^=S^+T^,\quad(aT)^=\overline aT^, (ST)^=T^S^,\qquad T^{}=T. For A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb C), its conjugate transpose is A^=\overline A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb C). In orthonormal bases \beta,\gamma, [T^]_\gamma^\beta=\bigl([T]_\beta^\gamma\bigr)^. An arbitrary nonorthonormal basis does not give this formula without accounting for the inner product. Useful identities are \ker T^=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp and \ker T=(\operatorname{im}T^)^\perp. For an operator, \det T^=\overline{\det T}. The algebraic dual map acts on functionals and uses a transpose, with no complex conjugation. It is a different construction. Links: Dual space · Dual basis and dual map · Orthogonal complement · Normal and self-adjoint operators · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 13 · 115A PDF, p. 14

title: Alternating Series Test
text: Theorem (Leibniz) If a_n\ge0, a_{n+1}\le a_n, and a_n\to0, then \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n a_n\quad\text{converges}. Proof idea: the even and odd partial sums are monotone in opposite directions, bound each other, and differ by a term tending to 0. Remainder estimate: if S is the sum and S_N the Nth partial sum, |S-S_N|\le a_{N+1}. Example: \sum(-1)^n/n converges conditionally. The test does not decide absolute convergence. Links: Absolute convergence · Partial sums · Monotone Convergence Theorem · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 10

title: Basis and dimension
text: Basis A basis \beta=(v_1,\ldots,v_n) of V is an independent spanning list. Every v\in V has a unique representation v=\sum_{j=1}^na_jv_j,\qquad[v]_\beta=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^{\mathsf T}. The coordinate map v\mapsto[v]_\beta is an isomorphism V\to\mathbb F^n. Coordinates depend on the ordered basis. For a finite-dimensional space, all bases have the same length, called \dim V. The zero space has the empty basis and dimension 0. Basis extension: an independent list can be extended to a basis; a finite spanning list can be reduced to a basis. Consequently, in an n-dimensional space: - an independent list has at most n vectors; - a spanning list has at least n vectors; - a list of exactly n vectors is a basis iff it is independent, iff it spans. Proof idea: when a spanning list is dependent, remove a redundant vector. To extend an independent list, keep adding a vector outside its span; finite dimension forces the process to stop. For \mathcal P_m(\mathbb F)=\{p:\deg p\le m\}\cup\{0\}, (1,x,\ldots,x^m) is a basis, so the dimension is m+1. Links: Span and linear independence · Matrix representation · Rank-nullity theorem · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 4

title: Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem
text: Theorem Every bounded sequence in \mathbb R^d has a convergent subsequence. Proof in \mathbb R: choose a monotone subsequence, then apply Monotone Convergence Theorem. In finite-dimensional \mathbb R^d, successively extract subsequences for each coordinate. Where is the limit? A bounded sequence in E has a subsequence converging somewhere in \mathbb R^d. If E is also closed, the limit lies in E. E\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ closed and bounded} \implies\text{every sequence in }E\text{ has a convergent subsequence with limit in }E. This is the sequential form of compactness. It resolves the original “?bdd???”: boundedness extracts a limit; closedness keeps it inside E. Counterexample: x_n=1/n\in(0,1] converges to 0\notin(0,1]. Links: Subsequence · Monotone Convergence Theorem · Compact set · limsup & liminf · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 4 · 131A PDF, p. 7

title: Branches of logarithms and powers
text: For z\ne0, all solutions of e^w=z are w=\log|z|+i(\operatorname{Arg}z+2\pi k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z. Principal branch On \Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0], take -\pi<\operatorname{Arg}z<\pi and define \operatorname{Log}z=\log|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}z. It is holomorphic, e^{\operatorname{Log}z}=z, and (\operatorname{Log}z)'=1/z. A logarithm branch on a domain D\subseteq\mathbb C\setminus\{0\} is a holomorphic function L with e^L=z. Two such branches differ by a constant 2\pi ik. A simply connected domain avoiding 0 admits a branch: integrate 1/z and choose the additive constant appropriately. No continuous logarithm exists on the whole punctured plane. Along z=e^{it}, continuity would force the imaginary part of a logarithm to increase by 2\pi after one turn, although the endpoint is unchanged. Once a branch L is fixed, define z^\alpha=e^{\alpha L(z)},\qquad (z^\alpha)'=\alpha e^{(\alpha-1)L(z)}. For square roots on \Omega, the branches are \pm e^{\operatorname{Log}z/2}. There is no continuous global square root on the punctured plane, by the same loop argument with a sign change. Example: all values of i^i are e^{-(\pi/2+2\pi k)}, k\in\mathbb Z; the principal value is e^{-\pi/2}. Boundary: logarithm and power identities depend on the branch. Even when all principal logarithms involved exist, \operatorname{Log}(zw) need not equal \operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w. Links: Complex numbers and polar form · Complex exponential and trigonometric functions · Domains and simple connectedness · Primitives and path independence · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 5 · 132 notes, p. 6 · 132 notes, p. 7 · 132 notes, p. 14 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Cauchy criterion for series
text: Theorem For a real or complex series \sum a_n, \sum a_n\text{ converges}\iff \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists N\ \forall mn\ge N: \left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{m}a_i\right|<\varepsilon. Proof: the displayed tail is |S_m-S_n| for partial sums S_n. Apply “Cauchy iff convergent” in \mathbb R or \mathbb C. Use: prove convergence without computing the sum. Small individual terms are insufficient; all sufficiently late finite tails must be small. Links: Cauchy sequence · Partial sums · Completeness Axiom · Absolute convergence · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 8

title: Cauchy estimates
text: Derivative bounds Suppose f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of \overline{D(a,r)}, with r0, and |f(z)|\le M on |z-a|=r. Then for n\ge0, |f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!M}{r^n}. Proof: combine Cauchy's derivative formula with the ML estimate: |f^{(n)}(a)|\le\frac{n!}{2\pi}\frac{M}{r^{n+1}}\,(2\pi r). For Taylor coefficients a_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!, this becomes |a_n|\le M/r^n. Use: if f is entire and globally bounded by the same M, take arbitrarily large r with n=1 to obtain f'(a)=0. This is Liouville's theorem. More generally, if |f(z)|\le C(1+|z|^m) for all z, with integer m\ge0, apply the estimate at 0 and let r\to\infty to see f^{(n)}(0)=0 for nm. The entire Taylor expansion makes f a polynomial of degree at most m. Boundary: an arbitrary entire function has a bound M_r on each circle, but M_r can grow with r. Letting r\to\infty only helps when that growth is controlled. Links: Cauchy integral formula · ML estimate · Liouville's theorem · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 31 · 132 notes, p. 32 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Cauchy integral formula
text: Let D be a bounded region whose boundary is a finite union of disjoint piecewise C^1 simple closed curves. Suppose f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of \overline D. Values and derivatives from the boundary For z\in D and n\ge0, f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\int_{\partial D}\frac{f(w)}{(w-z)^{n+1}}\,dw. The boundary has its full positive orientation, including clockwise boundaries of holes. The formula for n=0 determines every interior value from the boundary values. Proof route: remove a small disk centered at z and apply Cauchy's theorem to f(w)/(w-z). The outer boundary integral equals the integral over the small counterclockwise circle. Parametrize it and let its radius tend to zero to obtain 2\pi i f(z). Differentiating the kernel is justified uniformly on the fixed boundary, since an interior point has positive distance from it. Example from the notes: on the positive unit circle, put h(z)=e^{-z}/(z^2-4). It is holomorphic near the closed unit disk, and h'(0)=1/4. Hence \int_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{z^2(z^2-4)e^z} =2\pi i\,h'(0)=\frac{\pi i}{2}. Boundary: the point z must be inside D, and f must be regular throughout the required region. A singularity on the contour prevents direct use of this formula. Links: Cauchy's theorem · Cauchy estimates · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Residue · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 28 · 132 notes, p. 29 · 132 notes, p. 30 · 132 notes, p. 31 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Cauchy sequence
text: Definition A sequence in a metric space (X,d) is Cauchy if \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\ge N:\ d(x_n,x_m)<\varepsilon. In \mathbb R, d(x_n,x_m)=|x_n-x_m|. Intuition: terms eventually get close to each other; the definition does not name a limit. By the Completeness Axiom, \text{in }\mathbb R:\qquad\text{Cauchy}\iff\text{convergent}. In any metric space: convergent \implies Cauchy \implies bounded. The first converse holds in a complete space; boundedness alone gives neither Cauchy nor convergence. Counterexamples: (-1)^n is bounded but not Cauchy; rational approximations to \sqrt2 are Cauchy in \mathbb Q but do not converge there. Links: Convergence of a sequence · Completeness Axiom · Cauchy criterion for series · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 2 · 131A PDF, p. 3

title: Cauchy-Riemann equations
text: Write f(x+iy)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y). Cauchy-Riemann Complex differentiability at a point implies u_x=v_y,\qquad u_y=-v_x, and f'=u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y there. Proof idea: take the difference quotient first along real increments and then along imaginary increments. Both limits must equal the same complex derivative. Conversely, if u,v are real differentiable at a point and satisfy these equations there, their real linear approximation is multiplication by u_x+iv_x, so f is complex differentiable there. In particular, if u,v\in C^1(U) and the equations hold throughout an open set U, then f is holomorphic on U. Why regularity matters: put u(0,0)=0, u(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2) elsewhere, and v=0. All four partial derivatives at 0 vanish, so the equations hold there, but f=u is not even continuous at 0. For local polar coordinates z=re^{i\theta} with r0, u_r=\frac1r v_\theta,\qquad u_\theta=-r v_r. These follow from the real chain rule. They do not give a coordinate formula at r=0. Consequence: if both f and \overline f are holomorphic on a domain, all first partial derivatives vanish, so f is constant. Links: Holomorphic functions · Complex inverse function theorem · Harmonic functions · Complex limits and continuity · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 10 · 132 notes, p. 11 · 132 notes, p. 12 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
text: Cauchy-Schwarz In a real or complex inner-product space, |\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|. Equality holds iff x,y are linearly dependent, including the case where one is zero. Proof: for y\ne0, subtract the component along y: 0\le\left\|x-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\|y\|^2}y\right\|^2 =\|x\|^2-\frac{|\langle x,y\rangle|^2}{\|y\|^2}. Equality means the residual is zero. The case y=0 is immediate. It implies the triangle inequality by \|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2 \le(\|x\|+\|y\|)^2. Every inner-product norm also satisfies \|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2. In a real inner-product space, for nonzero x,y, define the angle by \cos\theta=\langle x,y\rangle/(\|x\|\|y\|). The same formula without taking account of complex values is not a real angle formula on a complex space. Applying the inequality to the integral inner product gives the version used in Riemann integral and L2 space. Links: Inner product · Orthogonal projection · Riemann integral · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 9

title: Cauchy's theorem
text: Boundary version Let D be a bounded region whose boundary consists of finitely many disjoint piecewise C^1 simple closed curves. If f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of \overline D, then \int_{\partial D}f(z)\,dz=0. Use the complete positive boundary: the outer curve is counterclockwise and each inner curve is clockwise. No simple connectedness is needed for this boundary statement. Proof idea: write f=u+iv and apply Green's theorem to f\,dz=(u\,dx-v\,dy)+i(v\,dx+u\,dy). Cauchy-Riemann makes both area integrands zero. Goursat's theorem supplies the theorem without separately assuming continuity of f'. Simply connected version: if f is holomorphic on a simply connected domain U, its integral around every piecewise smooth closed path in U is zero. Equivalently, it has a primitive there. One obtains this version from the local integral theorem by subdividing a contraction of the path. Hole example: for 0<r<R and f(z)=1/z, 0=\int_{\partial\{r<|z|<R\}}\frac{dz}{z} =\int_{|z|=R}\frac{dz}{z}-\int_{|z|=r}\frac{dz}{z}, where both displayed circles on the right are counterclockwise. Boundary: being holomorphic only near a closed curve is insufficient to make its integral zero. The interior obstruction at 0 gives \int_{|z|=1}dz/z=2\pi i. Links: Green's theorem and exact forms · Goursat's theorem · Primitives and path independence · Cauchy integral formula · Residue theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 26 · 132 notes, p. 27 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Cayley-Hamilton theorem
text: Cayley-Hamilton Every operator on a finite-dimensional vector space satisfies its characteristic polynomial: \chi_T(T)=0. Here \chi_T(t)=\det(tI-[T]). If \chi_T(t)=t^n+c_{n-1}t^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0, the statement means T^n+c_{n-1}T^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0I=0. Constants become scalar multiples of I. Proof route: for each v\ne0, the restriction to Z(v,T) has characteristic polynomial p_v and satisfies p_v(T)v=0 by the companion-matrix description. Since this subspace is invariant, p_v divides \chi_T. Hence \chi_T(T)v=0 for every v. For a 2\times2 matrix, A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=0. If \det A\ne0, this gives A^{-1}=\frac{(\operatorname{tr}A)I-A}{\det A}. More generally, powers of T can be reduced to combinations of I,T,\ldots,T^{n-1}. The minimal polynomial can make this reduction shorter. The theorem works over any field. It does not assume that the characteristic polynomial splits or that T is diagonalizable. Links: Cyclic subspace · Invariant subspace · Determinant and trace · Minimal polynomial · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Diagonalization

title: Change of basis and similarity
text: Let T:V\to V with \dim V=n, and let \beta,\gamma be ordered bases. Put P=\begin{bmatrix}[\gamma_1]_\beta&\cdots&[\gamma_n]_\beta\end{bmatrix}. Then [v]_\beta=P[v]_\gamma: P converts new coordinates to old coordinates. Similarity If A=[T]_\beta and B=[T]_\gamma, then B=P^{-1}AP. Apply P to enter old coordinates, apply A, then P^{-1} to return. This order prevents most change-of-basis mistakes. Similar matrices have the same characteristic and minimal polynomials, determinant, trace, rank, nullity and eigenvalue multiplicities. Their kernels and images need not be the same coordinate subsets: \ker B=P^{-1}(\ker A),\qquad\operatorname{im}B=P^{-1}(\operatorname{im}A). For example, swapping the coordinates changes the kernel of \operatorname{diag}(0,1) from the first coordinate axis to the second. When domain and codomain bases change independently, the general rule is A_{\mathrm{new}}=Q^{-1}AP. Similarity uses the same change on both sides. A quadratic form instead changes by congruence P^{\mathsf T}AP. Links: Matrix representation · Determinant and trace · Diagonalization · Quadratic form · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 5

title: Compact set
text: Let K be a subset of a metric space (X,d). Definition (open cover) K is compact if every cover by open sets in X has a finite subcover: K\subseteq\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}U_\alpha \implies\exists\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m: K\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^mU_{\alpha_j}. Sequential characterization (metric spaces) K is compact iff every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point in K. Heine–Borel (Euclidean space) K\subseteq\mathbb R^d:\qquad K\text{ compact}\iff K\text{ closed and bounded}. For general metric spaces, compact \implies closed and bounded, but the converse fails. An infinite set with discrete metric d(x,y)=1 for x\ne y is closed and bounded in itself, yet its singleton open cover has no finite subcover. Stability: finite unions of compact sets are compact; a relatively closed subset of a compact set is compact; a nonempty finite family of compact sets has compact intersection. Compactness + continuity Let f:K\to Y be continuous, with Y metric. - Continuous image: f(K) is compact. Pull an open cover back by f, select a finite subcover of K, then map it forward. - Extreme Value Theorem: if K\ne\varnothing and f:K\to\mathbb R, f attains a maximum and minimum. Indeed, f(K) is nonempty, closed and bounded in \mathbb R, so it contains its sup and inf. - Heine–Cantor: f is uniformly continuous on K. Proof map and counterexamples: Compactness and continuity. Links: Open & closed · Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem · Uniform continuity · Nested Closed Sets Theorem · Continuity · 131A · 131B Source: 131A PDF, p. 5 · 131A PDF, p. 7 · 131A PDF, p. 13

title: Compactness and continuity
text: 核心问题：什么时候可以从“每个点附近有控制”，得到整个定义域上的控制？ 先固定空间和量词 | 概念 | 假设与结论 | 注意 | |---|---|---| | Compact | 每个 open cover 有 finite subcover | 定义不依赖 Euclidean 坐标 | | Sequential compactness | 每个序列都有子列收敛到集合内 | 在 metric spaces 中等价于 compact | | Heine–Borel | K\subseteq\mathbb R^d: compact iff closed and bounded | 一般 metric space 不能使用反向 | | Continuity | \forall x_0\ \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall x | \delta 可以依赖 x_0 | | Uniform continuity | \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall x,y | 一个 \delta 同时适用于全部点 | 完整定义：Compact set · Continuity · Continuity in metric spaces · Uniform continuity。 三条证明路线 1. Compact domain + continuous map → compact image 设 K compact，f:K\to Y continuous。对 f(K) 的任意 open cover \{U_\alpha\}： f(K)\subseteq\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha \implies K\subseteq\bigcup_\alpha f^{-1}(U_\alpha). 连续性保证 preimages 在 K 中相对开；compactness 选出有限个： K\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^m f^{-1}(U_{\alpha_j}) \implies f(K)\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^m U_{\alpha_j}. 2. Nonempty compact domain + real-valued continuity → extrema \varnothing\ne K\text{ compact},\quad f:K\to\mathbb R\text{ continuous} \implies f(K)\text{ nonempty, closed, bounded} \implies \sup f(K),\inf f(K)\in f(K). 于是存在 x_{\max},x_{\min}\in K 取得最大、最小值。这里需要的是实数像空间的序结构，以及非空定义域。 3. Compact metric domain + continuity → uniform continuity 反设不是 uniformly continuous，则 \exists\varepsilon_00\ \forall n\ \exists x_n,y_n\in K: \quad d_X(x_n,y_n)<1/n,\quad d_Y(f(x_n),f(y_n))\ge\varepsilon_0. 由 sequential compactness，选 x_{n_k}\to x\in K。于是 d_X(y_{n_k},x)\le d_X(y_{n_k},x_{n_k})+d_X(x_{n_k},x)\to0, d_Y(f(x_{n_k}),f(y_{n_k})) \le d_Y(f(x_{n_k}),f(x))+d_Y(f(x),f(y_{n_k}))\to0, 矛盾。这就是 Heine–Cantor；不要求像空间 complete。 哪个条件不能省 | 例子 | 成立 | 失败或提醒 | |---|---|---| | 1/x on (0,1) | Continuous | 不 uniformly continuous；定义域 bounded 但不 compact | | f(x)=x on (0,1) | Lipschitz、bounded | 不取得 max/min；uniform continuity 不保证 extrema | | \sqrt{x} on [0,1] | Compact domain、uniformly continuous | 不 Lipschitz | | \mathbb N with discrete metric | Closed in itself、bounded、complete | 不 compact；无限 singleton cover 无 finite subcover | | f(n)=n from discrete \mathbb N to \mathbb R | Uniformly continuous | 像无界；一般 bounded metric domain 不足以保证 bounded image | 最后两行说明：在 \mathbb R^d 中成立的“closed + bounded”或“bounded domain”推论，需要逐条检查才能推广。 接着连到哪里 - Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem：boundedness 提取收敛子列，closedness 把极限留在集合内。 - Nested Closed Sets Theorem：在同一个 compact set 内，嵌套的非空闭集不能全部消失。 - Connectedness → IVT：connectedness 保证中间值；compactness 保证极值，作用不同。 - Uniform continuity → Cauchy sequence：Cauchy sequences 的像仍是 Cauchy；值域 complete 时才能据此建立端点延拓。 - Uniform convergence：这里统一的是函数列的 N，与 uniform continuity 统一 \delta 的量词结构相似。 Sources: 131A p. 7 · 131A p. 11 · 131A p. 13 · 131B p. 1。 证明路线与反例为本次校对整理；原 PDF 页码用于定位相关主题。

title: Comparison test
text: Theorem (nonnegative terms) Suppose 0\le b_n\le a_n for all sufficiently large n. - \sum a_n convergent \implies\sum b_n convergent. - \sum b_n divergent \implies\sum a_n divergent. Reason: nonnegative partial sums are monotone; the inequality transfers an upper bound or forces divergence to +\infty. Absolute comparison If |b_n|\le a_n eventually and \sum a_n converges, then \sum b_n converges absolutely, hence converges. Changing finitely many terms does not affect convergence. For signed terms, b_n\le a_n alone is not the absolute comparison hypothesis. Links: Absolute convergence · Partial sums · Root test · Ratio test · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 9

title: Completeness Axiom
text: Course axiom Every Cauchy sequence in \mathbb R converges to a point of \mathbb R. 131A takes this as an axiom. If \mathbb R is first constructed using Dedekind cuts, completeness can instead be proved for that construction. Equivalent formulations for \mathbb R (with its usual ordered-field structure and Archimedean property): 1. Every Cauchy sequence converges in \mathbb R. 2. Every nonempty subset bounded above has a least upper bound in \mathbb R. 3. Every bounded monotone real sequence converges. Why \mathbb Q fails: rational decimal truncations 1,1.4,1.41,1.414,\ldots of \sqrt2 are Cauchy, but their limit is not rational. Links: Dedekind cut · Sup & inf · Cauchy sequence · Monotone Convergence Theorem · Completeness of a metric space · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 2 · 131A PDF, p. 3

title: Completeness of a metric space
text: Definition A metric space (X,d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. \mathbb R, \mathbb R^d are complete; \mathbb Q is not. Completeness generalizes the Completeness Axiom for \mathbb R. Bounded functions with the sup metric For a nonempty set S, define B(S,\mathbb R)=\{f:S\to\mathbb R:f\text{ bounded}\},\qquad d_\infty(f,g)=\sup_{x\in S}|f(x)-g(x)|. Theorem (B(S,\mathbb R),d_\infty) is complete. Proof: if (f_n) is sup-Cauchy, then (f_n(x)) is real-Cauchy for each x, so define f(x)=\lim_n f_n(x). Given \varepsilon0, choose N so that n,m\ge N gives \sup_S|f_n-f_m|<\varepsilon/2. Let m\to\infty pointwise: |f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\varepsilon/2\quad\forall x,\ n\ge N. Thus f_n\rightrightarrows f. Taking one sufficiently late f_N gives |f(x)|\le |f_N(x)|+1, so f is bounded. Subspaces - A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete. - A complete metric subspace is closed in its ambient metric space: a convergent sequence from the subspace is Cauchy, and uniqueness identifies its limit with the subspace limit. - Every compact metric space is complete: extract a convergent subsequence of a Cauchy sequence, then use Cauchy to bring the whole sequence to the same limit. Complete does not imply compact; an infinite discrete metric space is a counterexample. Links: Metric space · Cauchy sequence · Open & closed · Spaces of functions · Compact set · 131B Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Complex exponential and trigonometric functions
text: e^z=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{n!},\qquad e^{x+iy}=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y). The series has infinite radius of convergence, so e^z is entire and (e^z)'=e^z. e^{z+w}=e^ze^w,\qquad |e^z|=e^{\operatorname{Re}z},\qquad e^z\ne0. Also e^z=e^w iff z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z. Thus the exponential is locally invertible everywhere but is not globally injective on \mathbb C. Complex sine and cosine \sin z=\frac{e^{iz}-e^{-iz}}{2i} =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nz^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}, \cos z=\frac{e^{iz}+e^{-iz}}2 =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nz^{2n}}{(2n)!}. Both are entire, with (\sin z)'=\cos z, (\cos z)'=-\sin z and \sin^2z+\cos^2z=1. Boundary: the real-variable bounds do not extend to \mathbb C. For real y, \cos(iy)=\frac{e^{-y}+e^y}{2}, which is unbounded as |y|\to\infty. Links: Branches of logarithms and powers · Complex power series · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Fourier coefficients · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 6 · 132 notes, p. 11 · 132 notes, p. 43 · 132 notes, p. 44 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Complex inverse function theorem
text: Local inverse Suppose f is holomorphic near a and f'(a)\ne0. There are neighborhoods U of a and V of f(a) such that f:U\to V is bijective and its inverse is holomorphic. \bigl(f^{-1}\bigr)'(w)=\frac1{f'(f^{-1}(w))}\qquad(w\in V). Write f'=p+iq. The Cauchy-Riemann equations give the real Jacobian Df=\begin{pmatrix}p&-q\\q&p\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det Df=p^2+q^2=|f'|^2. Use the real inverse function theorem. For w=f(z) and w_0=f(z_0), \frac{f^{-1}(w)-f^{-1}(w_0)}{w-w_0} =\frac{z-z_0}{f(z)-f(z_0)}\longrightarrow\frac1{f'(z_0)}. The same matrix is a rotation followed by scaling when f'\ne0: this explains local angle preservation at regular points. Example: e^z has nonzero derivative everywhere. Each local inverse is a logarithm branch, with derivative 1/z. Boundary: e^{z+2\pi i}=e^z, so nonzero derivative everywhere does not imply global injectivity. The inverse theorem requires f holomorphic on a neighborhood, not merely differentiable at the single point. title: Complex limits and continuity
text: For z_n,z\in\mathbb C, z_n\to z\iff |z_n-z|\to0\iff \operatorname{Re}z_n\to\operatorname{Re}z\text{ and }\operatorname{Im}z_n\to\operatorname{Im}z. The complex plane is complete: a sequence converges iff it is Cauchy, by applying real completeness to its two coordinates. Function limit Let f:E\to\mathbb C and let a be a limit point of E. Then \lim_{z\to a}f(z)=L means \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall z\in E: 0<|z-a|<\delta\implies |f(z)-L|<\varepsilon. Equivalently, f(z_n)\to L for every sequence z_n\in E\setminus\{a\} tending to a. Continuity at a\in E uses the same estimate without excluding z=a, with L=f(a). At an isolated point it holds automatically. Sums and products preserve limits; quotients do when the limiting denominator is nonzero. Boundary: agreement along the real and imaginary axes is insufficient. For f(x+iy)=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}\qquad(x+iy\ne0), both axes give 0, while the line y=x gives 1/2. A complex limit must work for every approach within the domain. Links: Convergence of a sequence · Cauchy sequence · Continuity in metric spaces · Holomorphic functions · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 7 · 132 notes, p. 8 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Complex numbers and polar form
text: For z=x+iy, with x,y\in\mathbb R, \overline z=x-iy,\qquad |z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad z\overline z=|z|^2. Polar form For z\ne0, write z=re^{i\theta}, where r=|z|0 and e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta. All arguments differ by 2\pi k, k\in\mathbb Z; choose \operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi] as the principal argument. Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments: r_1e^{i\theta_1}r_2e^{i\theta_2}=r_1r_2e^{i(\theta_1+\theta_2)}. Thus (e^{i\theta})^n=e^{in\theta} for n\in\mathbb Z. If n\ge1 and z=re^{i\theta}\ne0, its n distinct nth roots are r^{1/n}e^{i(\theta+2\pi k)/n},\qquad k=0,\ldots,n-1. For n\ge2, the nth roots of unity sum to 0, by the finite geometric sum. Useful estimates: |z+w|\le |z|+|w|,\qquad \bigl||z|-|w|\bigr|\le |z-w|. Equality in the first holds exactly when one number is zero or the two nonzero numbers have the same argument modulo 2\pi. Boundary: 0 has no argument. The principal argument has a jump across the negative real axis; choosing a principal value does not make it globally continuous. Links: Branches of logarithms and powers · Complex exponential and trigonometric functions · Complex limits and continuity · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 2 · 132 notes, p. 3 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Complex power series
text: For a_n,a\in\mathbb C, consider \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(z-a)^n. Radius of convergence R=\frac1{\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}},\qquad 1/0=\infty,\quad1/\infty=0. The series converges absolutely for |z-a|<R, and diverges for |z-a|R. At z=a it always equals a_0, even if R=0. For 0<R<\infty, points on the boundary circle require separate examination. If R0, convergence is uniform on each closed disk |z-a|\le r<R, hence locally uniform on D(a,R). Choose r<s<R; boundedness of |a_n|s^n gives a geometric majorant C(r/s)^n, and apply the M-test. The sum is holomorphic, and termwise differentiation gives f^{(m)}(z)=\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}\frac{n!}{(n-m)!}a_n(z-a)^{n-m}. Each differentiated series has the same radius and converges locally uniformly inside it. Examples: \sum z^n and \sum nz^n have radius 1; \sum z^n/n! has infinite radius. Convergence on every smaller closed disk does not assert uniform convergence on the entire open convergence disk. Compare the real-variable card: an interval has two endpoints to check, while a complex disk has a whole boundary circle. Links: Power series · Root test · Weierstrass M-test · Locally uniform convergence · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 35 · 132 notes, p. 39 · 132 notes, p. 40 · 132 notes, p. 41 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Connectedness
text: Let E be a metric space, or a subset with its induced metric. Definition E is disconnected if E=U\cup V for disjoint, nonempty sets U,V open relative to E. Otherwise E is connected. In \mathbb R: a nonempty subset is connected iff it is an interval, allowing singletons. The empty set is also connected by the definition. Continuous images preserve connectedness If E is connected and f:E\to Y continuous, then f(E) is connected. Proof: a separation of f(E) pulls back to a separation of E. For a real-valued continuous map on [a,b], this gives IVT: the image is an interval, so it contains every value between f(a) and f(b). Path connectedness E is path connected if for any x,y\in E there is a continuous \gamma:[0,1]\to E with \gamma(0)=x, \gamma(1)=y. \text{path connected}\implies\text{connected}. The converse holds for subsets of \mathbb R (use the line segment inside an interval). It fails in \mathbb R^2: the topologist's sine curve E=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}\cup(\{0\}\times[-1,1]) is connected but not path connected. The oscillating graph is connected and its closure is E; there is no path from the vertical segment to the graph. Links: IVT · Continuity in metric spaces · Open & closed · 131B · Domains and simple connectedness Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Continuity
text: Let f:E\to\mathbb R, E\subseteq\mathbb R, and fix x_0\in E. Definition f is continuous at x_0 if \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall x\in E: |x-x_0|<\delta\implies|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon. \delta may depend on \varepsilon and the fixed x_0, but must work for every x in that neighborhood. Continuity on E means continuity at every x_0\in E. Sequential criterion: for every (x_n)\subseteq E, x_n\to x_0\implies f(x_n)\to f(x_0). For general metrics and the open-preimage criterion, see Continuity in metric spaces. Algebra: continuous real-valued f,g on E give continuous f+g, fg, and f/g wherever g\ne0. If g:E\to F and h:F\to\mathbb R are continuous, so is h\circ g. Compact domain: a continuous image of a compact set is compact. If the domain is also nonempty and the map real-valued, it attains max/min. Heine–Cantor supplies one \delta for all base points. Counterexample to continuity \Rightarrow uniform continuity: f(x)=1/x on (0,1); take x_n=1/(n+1) and y_n=1/(n+2). Their distance tends to 0, but |f(x_n)-f(y_n)|=1. Links: Uniform continuity · IVT · Compact set · Compactness and continuity · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 11 · 131A PDF, p. 12 · 131A PDF, p. 13

title: Continuity in metric spaces
text: Let f:(X,d_X)\to(Y,d_Y) and fix x_0\in X. At one point The following are equivalent: 1. Epsilon–delta: \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall x\in X: d_X(x,x_0)<\delta\implies d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon. 2. Sequential: for every sequence (x_n) in X, x_n\to x_0\implies f(x_n)\to f(x_0). \delta=\delta(\varepsilon,x_0) may depend on the fixed base point. Reversing the order to choose one \delta before all base points is Uniform continuity. On the whole space Open-preimage criterion f is continuous at every point of X iff f^{-1}(U) is open in X for every open U\subseteq Y. Proof direction: if x\in f^{-1}(U), choose a ball around f(x) contained in U; continuity gives a ball around x contained in its preimage. Conversely, take U=B_Y(f(x_0),\varepsilon) and use openness of its preimage. It is the preimage that stays open. A continuous map need not send open sets to open sets: a constant map \mathbb R\to\mathbb R sends \mathbb R to a singleton. Connections: Lipschitz continuity \Rightarrow Uniform continuity \Rightarrow continuity. Compact domains give the middle condition by Heine–Cantor. Links: Continuity · Metric space · Open & closed · Compactness and continuity · 131B Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Contour integrals
text: Let \gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C be a piecewise C^1 path and f continuous on its image. Complex line integral \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=\int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt. For f=u+iv and z=x+iy, f(z)\,dz=(u\,dx-v\,dy)+i(v\,dx+u\,dy). The definition is independent of an orientation-preserving piecewise smooth reparametrization. Reversing the path changes the sign; concatenation adds the integrals. Arc length instead uses L(\gamma)=\int_a^b|\gamma'(t)|\,dt=\int_\gamma|dz|. The complex element dz records direction; |dz| measures length. Circle example: for the positively oriented circle \gamma(t)=a+re^{it}, 0\le t\le2\pi, with r0, \int_\gamma(z-a)^m\,dz= \begin{cases}2\pi i,&m=-1,\\0,&m\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{-1\}.\end{cases} Substitute dz=ire^{it}\,dt and integrate ir^{m+1}e^{i(m+1)t}. Traversing the circle clockwise reverses the result; multiple traversals multiply it by the signed number of turns. Boundary: a closed path does not by itself make a contour integral zero. The case m=-1 is the basic obstruction to a global primitive. Links: Riemann integral · ML estimate · Primitives and path independence · Residue · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 17 · 132 notes, p. 20 · 132 notes, p. 21 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Convergence of a sequence
text: Definition A real sequence (x_n) converges to x\in\mathbb R if \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N:\ |x_n-x|<\varepsilon. Write x_n\to x or \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=x. In a metric space, use d(x_n,x) in place of |x_n-x| and require x\in X. Infinite limits for real sequences x_n\to+\infty\iff\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N:\ x_nM. x_n\to-\infty\iff\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N:\ x_n<M. These are extended-real limits, not convergence to a point of \mathbb R. Key facts - Every convergent sequence is bounded. ^fact-conv-bounded - The limit is unique. - Convergent \implies Cauchy in every metric space; the converse requires completeness. Links: Cauchy sequence · Monotone Convergence Theorem · Subsequence · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 1 · 131A PDF, p. 3

title: Convolution
text: Periodic setting For f,g\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), \mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, define (fg)(x)=\int_0^1f(x-t)g(t)\,dt =\int_0^1f(t)g(x-t)\,dt. The equality follows by substitution and periodicity. Convolution is a weighted average of translates when g\ge0 and \int_0^1g=1. A positive approximate identity Suppose continuous periodic kernels K_j satisfy K_j\ge0,\qquad\int_0^1K_j(t)\,dt=1, \forall\eta\in(0,1/2):\quad \int_\eta^{1-\eta}K_j(t)\,dt\longrightarrow0. Then, for every f\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), fK_j\rightrightarrows f. Concentration is near 0 on the circle, hence near both ends of the coordinate interval [0,1]. Proof estimate: uniform continuity gives |f(x-t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon whenever the circle distance from t to 0 is <\eta. Therefore \|fK_j-f\|_\infty\le\varepsilon+ 2\|f\|_\infty\int_\eta^{1-\eta}K_j(t)\,dt. Trig-polynomial stability: if K(t)=\sum_{|n|\le N}b_ne_n(t), then fK=\sum_{|n|\le N}b_n\widehat f(n)e_n. This is the mechanism of Fourier theorem. Real-line setting For bounded uniformly continuous f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C and continuous compactly supported K, the integral (fK)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x-t)K(t)\,dt exists. If K_j\ge0, \int_{\mathbb R}K_j=1, and \int_{|t|\ge\eta}K_j\to0 for every \eta0, the same estimate gives uniform convergence to f. In particular this applies to continuous compactly supported f. It is not a uniform-convergence statement for arbitrary functions. Weierstrass Approximation Theorem specifies the extension and restricted interval needed for ordinary polynomial approximants. Links: Fourier coefficients · Fourier theorem · Weierstrass Approximation Theorem · Uniform continuity · 131B Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Cyclic subspace
text: Let T\in\mathcal L(V) with V finite-dimensional. The cyclic subspace generated by v is Z(v,T)=\operatorname{span}\{v,Tv,T^2v,\ldots\}. It is the smallest T-invariant subspace containing v. If v\ne0, let r be the first index for which T^rv lies in the span of its predecessors. Then \beta=(v,Tv,\ldots,T^{r-1}v) is a basis of Z(v,T), and there are unique a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1} such that T^rv=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}a_jT^jv. Companion matrix In this basis, T|_{Z(v,T)} has ones immediately below the diagonal, last column (a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1})^{\mathsf T}, and all other entries zero. Its characteristic and minimal polynomials are both p(t)=t^r-a_{r-1}t^{r-1}-\cdots-a_1t-a_0. The characteristic polynomial follows by expanding the companion determinant. Also p(T)v=0, so p(T) kills every T^jv; a smaller-degree relation would contradict independence of \beta. If Z(v,T)=V, then v is a cyclic vector for T. Not every operator has one: I on a space of dimension greater than 1 generates only a line from each nonzero vector. Links: Invariant subspace · Minimal polynomial · Cayley-Hamilton theorem · Matrix representation · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Diagonalization；Jordan / minimal poly

title: Dedekind cut
text:
Definition (lower cut) A Dedekind cut is S\subset\mathbb Q such that: 1. \varnothing
e S
e\mathbb Q; 2. r\in S,\ q\in\mathbb Q,\ q\le r\implies q\in S; 3. S has no maximum. Examples: a rational a corresponds to \{q\in\mathbb Q:q<a\}. The cut S=\{q\in\mathbb Q:q<0	ext{ or }q^2<2\} represents \sqrt2, even though \sqrt2
otin\mathbb Q. Upper-cut convention: instead use a nonempty proper upward-closed subset of \mathbb Q with no minimum. This is an alternative convention; the complement of a lower cut need not satisfy it (for rational a, the complement has minimum a). Payoff: the collection of lower cuts, with the appropriate order and arithmetic, constructs \mathbb R. This realizes the Completeness Axiom; a construction is not itself a completeness axiom. Links: Sup & inf · Completeness Axiom · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 1

title: Derivative
text: Definition For f:(a,b)\to\mathbb R and x\in(a,b), f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h, if this finite limit exists. Then f is differentiable at x. Geometric meaning: tangent slope / instantaneous rate of change. Differentiability implies continuity: f(x+h)-f(x)=h\left(f'(x)+o(1)\right)\to0. The converse fails for f(x)=|x| at 0. Monotonicity via MVT: for differentiable f on an interval, - f'\ge0\implies f nondecreasing; f'0\implies f strictly increasing. - f'\le0\implies f nonincreasing; f'<0\implies f strictly decreasing. - f'\equiv0\implies f constant. Strictly increasing does not require f'0 everywhere: x^3 has derivative 0 at 0. Links: Continuity · Local extrema · MVT · Lipschitz continuity · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 13 · 131A PDF, p. 14

title: Determinant and trace
text: For A\in M_n(\mathbb F), \operatorname{tr}A=\sum_{i=1}^na_{ii}. The determinant is alternating and multilinear in the rows (also in the columns), normalized by \det I=1. Basic identities: \det(AB)=\det A\det B,\qquad\det A^{\mathsf T}=\det A, A\text{ invertible}\iff\det A\ne0,\qquad\det A^{-1}=(\det A)^{-1}. The inverse formula assumes A is invertible. Cofactor expansion along row i is \det A=\sum_{j=1}^n(-1)^{i+j}a_{ij}\det A_{\widehat i,\widehat j}. Trace is linear; determinant is generally not linear as a function of the whole matrix. For example, \det(2I_n)=2^n over \mathbb R, not 2 when n1. The identity \operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA) and multiplicativity of determinant show both are invariant under similarity. They therefore define \operatorname{tr}T and \det T independently of a basis. If the characteristic polynomial splits over \mathbb F, list its roots \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n with algebraic multiplicity. Then \operatorname{tr}A=\sum_j\lambda_j,\qquad\det A=\prod_j\lambda_j. Splitting over \mathbb C does not make the roots real. Links: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces · Change of basis and similarity · Dual space · 115A · Complex inverse function theorem Source: 115A PDF, p. 5 · 115A PDF, p. 6 · 115B PDF, p. 1

title: Diagonalization
text: Definition T\in\mathcal L(V) is diagonalizable over \mathbb F if V has a basis of eigenvectors of T. For a matrix A, place these eigenvectors in the columns of P. Then A=PDP^{-1},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n). The jth diagonal entry corresponds to the jth column of P. For n=\dim V<\infty, the following are equivalent: - T is diagonalizable over \mathbb F; - V is the direct sum of its eigenspaces; - \sum_\lambda\dim E_\lambda=n; - \chi_T splits over \mathbb F and \dim E_\lambda=m_\lambda for every eigenvalue. Having n distinct eigenvalues is sufficient, not necessary: I_n is diagonalizable with only one eigenvalue when n1. Failure example: A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_1=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}. Its characteristic polynomial is (t-1)^2, but it has only one independent eigenvector. This nontrivial shear needs a Jordan block. Diagonalization does not generally give an orthonormal eigenbasis; that stronger conclusion is governed by the Spectral theorem. Links: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces · Change of basis and similarity · Direct sum · Minimal polynomial · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 5 · 115A PDF, p. 6 · 115A PDF, p. 7

title: Direct sum
text: For subspaces U,W\subseteq V, U+W=\{u+w:u\in U,\ w\in W\}. This is a subspace, generally different from the union U\cup W. Internal direct sum V=U\oplus W\iff V=U+W\text{ and }U\cap W=\{0\}. Equivalently, each v\in V has a unique decomposition v=u+w. Uniqueness follows because u+w=u'+w' puts u-u'=w'-w in the intersection. Conversely, a nonzero vector in the intersection gives two decompositions. If U,W are finite-dimensional, \dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W). For a direct sum, bases of the summands concatenate to a basis of V. Direct need not mean orthogonal: \mathbb R^2=\operatorname{span}(1,0)\oplus\operatorname{span}(1,1). An orthogonal decomposition is a special case, with an inner product supplying the complement. For more than two summands, require uniqueness of the whole sum, or U_j\cap\sum_{i\ne j}U_i=\{0\}. Pairwise zero intersections alone do not suffice: three distinct lines in \mathbb R^2 give a counterexample. Links: Subspace · Basis and dimension · Orthogonal complement · Generalized eigenspace · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Dual / Quotient

title: Domains and simple connectedness
text: Domain A domain D\subseteq\mathbb C is nonempty, open and connected. Every domain in \mathbb C is polygonally path connected. For a fixed point, the set of points reachable by polygonal paths is open, and its complement in D is open; use connectedness. A domain is simply connected if every continuous closed curve can be continuously contracted to a point while staying inside D. A domain is star-shaped about a\in D if a+t(z-a)\in D\qquad(z\in D,\ 0\le t\le1). Contract each loop along these segments to obtain \text{convex}\implies\text{star-shaped}\implies\text{simply connected}. Disks and \mathbb C are simply connected. The punctured plane and an annulus r<|z|<R, with 0<r<R, are connected but not simply connected: a circle around the missing center cannot contract there. Why it matters: holomorphic functions on a simply connected domain have primitives. A particular function can have a primitive on a domain with holes; for example, 1/z^2 has primitive -1/z on the punctured plane. Links: Connectedness · Open & closed · Primitives and path independence · Branches of logarithms and powers · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 4 · 132 notes, p. 18 · 132 notes, p. 24 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Dual basis and dual map
text: Let \beta=(v_1,\ldots,v_n) be a basis of V. Its dual basis \beta^=(f_1,\ldots,f_n) satisfies f_i(v_j)=\delta_{ij}. Thus f_i reads the ith coordinate: if v=\sum a_jv_j, then f_i(v)=a_i. For a basis matrix P=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n] in \mathbb F^n, f_i is represented by row i of P^{-1}. For the source's example, P=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-1/5&3/5\\2/5&-1/5\end{pmatrix}. So f_1(x,y)=(-x+3y)/5 and f_2(x,y)=(2x-y)/5. Dual map For T:V\to W, define T':W^\to V^ by T'(g)=g\circ T. If A=[T]_\beta^\gamma, then [T']_{\gamma^}^{\beta^}=A^{\mathsf T}. This is an ordinary transpose even over \mathbb C. The prime distinguishes this map from the inner-product adjoint T^; the source uses a star for both contexts. The evaluation map J:V\to V^{}, defined by J(v)(f)=f(v), is linear and injective. In finite dimension it is an isomorphism. Unlike a choice of V\cong V^, it requires no basis or inner product. Links: Dual space · Matrix representation · Adjoint · Isomorphism · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Dual / Quotient

title: Dual space
text: For a vector space V over \mathbb F, its algebraic dual is V^=\mathcal L(V,\mathbb F), the space of all linear functionals. A functional takes a vector as input and returns a scalar. Examples include coordinate functionals, evaluation f\mapsto f(a), and trace on M_n(\mathbb F). Determinant is generally not a linear functional. In finite dimension, \dim V^=\dim V; the coordinate-reading functionals associated with a basis form its dual basis. Inner-product representation (finite dimension) If V is a finite-dimensional inner-product space, every \varphi\in V^ has a unique representing vector y such that \varphi(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\quad(x\in V). For an orthonormal basis (e_j), take y=\sum_j\overline{\varphi(e_j)}e_j. This proves existence; testing the difference of two representing vectors proves uniqueness. With the first-argument-linear convention, y\mapsto\langle\cdot,y\rangle is conjugate-linear over \mathbb C, and linear over \mathbb R. It is not a canonical complex-linear identification V\to V^. In infinite dimension, the algebraic dual and the continuous dual need not coincide. Do not extend the finite-dimensional representation statement to every algebraic functional. Links: Linear map · Dual basis and dual map · Inner product · Adjoint · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 12 · 115A PDF, p. 13 · 115B PDF, p. 1

title: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces
text: Let T:V\to V be linear and finite-dimensional over \mathbb F. Eigenvector and eigenspace A nonzero v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \lambda\in\mathbb F if Tv=\lambda v. E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I). The eigenspace includes 0; an eigenvector does not. Using the monic convention, the characteristic polynomial is \chi_T(t)=\det(tI-[T]_\beta). It is basis-independent, has degree n=\dim V, and \lambda is an eigenvalue iff \chi_T(\lambda)=0. The convention \det([T]_\beta-tI) differs by (-1)^n. Multiplicities: geometric multiplicity is \dim E_\lambda; algebraic multiplicity m_\lambda is the multiplicity of \lambda as a root of \chi_T. 1\le\dim E_\lambda\le m_\lambda\quad\text{for an eigenvalue }\lambda. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent. To see the induction step, apply T-\lambda_kI to a shortest alleged dependence. Field matters: a 90^\circ rotation has no real eigenvalues, but has eigenvalues i,-i over \mathbb C. If Tv=\lambda v, then p(T)v=p(\lambda)v for every polynomial p. Links: Kernel and image · Determinant and trace · Diagonalization · Generalized eigenspace · 115A · Fundamental theorem of algebra Source: 115A PDF, p. 6 · 115A PDF, p. 7

title: Essential singularities
text: An isolated singularity is essential when its Laurent principal part has infinitely many nonzero terms. Example: e^{1/z}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac1{n!z^n}\qquad(z\ne0). It has an essential singularity at 0. Along positive real z\to0 it tends to infinity, while along negative real z\to0 it tends to 0. Casorati-Weierstrass If a is an essential singularity of f, then the image of every sufficiently small punctured disk 0<|z-a|<r is dense in \mathbb C. Proof idea: if the image missed a disk D(w,\varepsilon), then g(z)=\frac1{f(z)-w} would be bounded on that punctured disk. Extend g across a using the removable singularity theorem. If g(a)\ne0, then f=w+1/g extends holomorphically. If g(a)=0, its zero has finite order, so f has a pole. Both contradict essentiality. Boundary: dense image does not mean every value is attained; e^{1/z} never equals 0. The conclusion concerns every small punctured neighborhood, not merely the image on some large domain. Links: Isolated singularities · Laurent series · Removable singularity theorem · Zeros of holomorphic functions · Liouville's theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 53 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Fourier coefficients
text: Work with f\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), \mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, and the inner product in L2 space. Modes and coefficients e_n(x)=e^{2\pi inx},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z, \langle e_n,e_m\rangle=\int_0^1e^{2\pi i(n-m)x}\,dx=\delta_{nm}, \widehat f(n)=\langle f,e_n\rangle=\int_0^1f(x)e^{-2\pi inx}\,dx. \widehat f(n) is the component of f in frequency n. Orthogonal projection Let V_N=\operatorname{span}\{e_{-N},\ldots,e_N\} and F_N(x)=\sum_{n=-N}^{N}\widehat f(n)e_n(x). Then f-F_N is orthogonal to V_N. For every P\in V_N, \|f-P\|_2^2=\|f-F_N\|_2^2+\|F_N-P\|_2^2, so F_N is the best L^2 approximation in V_N. This finite projection identity does not assert uniform convergence of F_N. Fourier theorem gives uniform approximation by Fejér means; Parseval identity explains L^2 convergence of the ordinary partial sums. Links: L2 space · Fourier theorem · Parseval identity · Convolution · 131B · Orthogonal projection · Complex exponential and trigonometric functions · Real integrals by residues Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Fourier theorem
text: Uniform density of trigonometric polynomials For f\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), \mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, and every \varepsilon0, there is a trigonometric polynomial P with \|f-P\|_\infty<\varepsilon. Fejér approximation An explicit choice comes from the Fejér kernel K_N(t)=\frac1{N+1}\left|\sum_{k=0}^Ne^{2\pi ikt}\right|^2 =\sum_{|n|\le N}\left(1-\frac{|n|}{N+1}\right)e^{2\pi int}. It is nonnegative, has integral 1, and its mass away from 0 on the circle tends to 0. Thus Convolution gives \sigma_Nf=fK_N =\sum_{|n|\le N}\left(1-\frac{|n|}{N+1}\right)\widehat f(n)e_n \rightrightarrows f. If F_j is the ordinary jth Fourier partial sum, then \sigma_Nf=(N+1)^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^NF_j. Distinction: this proves uniform convergence of the Fejér means, not of the ordinary partial sums F_N. Continuity alone does not guarantee uniform convergence of F_N. Connection to L^2: for continuous periodic functions, \|f-P\|_2\le\|f-P\|_\infty. Combining density with the best-approximation property of F_N yields F_N\to f in L^2 and Parseval identity. Extending density to all of Lebesgue L^2 additionally uses density of continuous functions there. The ordinary-polynomial counterpart is Weierstrass Approximation Theorem. Links: Convolution · Fourier coefficients · Parseval identity · L2 space · 131B Supplementary check: [A. Seeger, Some approximation theorems in Math 522, pp. 2–4](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~aseeger/522/fejer.pdfpage=2). The formulas here use period 1 rather than 2\pi. Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Fundamental theorem of algebra
text: Fundamental theorem of algebra Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root. Consequently, a degree-n polynomial factors into n linear factors over \mathbb C, counted with multiplicity. Proof from Liouville: let p have positive degree and suppose it has no zero. Then 1/p is entire. The leading term gives |p(z)|\to\infty\qquad(|z|\to\infty), so 1/p is bounded outside a sufficiently large disk. Inside the closed disk it is continuous and therefore bounded by compactness. Liouville makes 1/p, hence p, constant, a contradiction. Factor out one root and repeat. Linear algebra connection: the characteristic polynomial of an operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space has a root, so the operator has an eigenvalue. The polynomial splits over \mathbb C, allowing Jordan form; this alone does not imply diagonalizability. Boundary: the statement depends on the field. The polynomial t^2+1 has no real root, and a real rotation can have no real eigenvalue. Links: Liouville's theorem · Compact set · Eigenvalues and eigenspaces · Jordan canonical form · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 1 · 132 notes, p. 33

title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
text: Let a<b be finite and f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R). Part 1 If F(x)=\int_a^xf(t)\,dt, then F is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(a<x<b). At the endpoints the corresponding one-sided derivatives equal f(a),f(b). Proof idea: \frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h-f(x)=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}(f(t)-f(x))\,dt, whose absolute value is bounded by the oscillation of f between x and x+h, tending to 0. Part 2 If G is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and G'=f there, then \int_a^bf(x)\,dx=G(b)-G(a). Proof: Part 1 gives F'=f, so (G-F)'=0. MVT makes G-F constant. Links: Riemann integral · Derivative · MVT · 131B · Primitives and path independence Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Generalized eigenspace
text: Let T\in\mathcal L(V), n=\dim V<\infty, and \lambda\in\mathbb F. Generalized eigenvector A nonzero v is a generalized eigenvector for \lambda if (T-\lambda I)^kv=0\quad\text{for some }k\ge1. The kernels form an increasing chain that stabilizes by k=n. Thus the generalized eigenspace is G_\lambda=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\ker(T-\lambda I)^k=\ker(T-\lambda I)^n. It contains the ordinary eigenspace E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I). G_\lambda is invariant, and N_\lambda=(T-\lambda I)|_{G_\lambda} is nilpotent. The restriction matters: T-\lambda I need not be nilpotent on all of V. If \chi_T splits over \mathbb F, then V=\bigoplus_\lambda G_\lambda,\qquad\dim G_\lambda=m_\lambda. The factors (t-\lambda)^{m_\lambda} are pairwise coprime; polynomial Bezout identities separate the corresponding components. Each restriction is \lambda I+N_\lambda, leading to Jordan canonical form. Example: for A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, E_1=\operatorname{span}e_1,\qquad G_1=\mathbb F^2, and (A-I)e_2=e_1, (A-I)e_1=0. For a diagonalizable operator, G_\lambda=E_\lambda; generalized eigenvectors add no new directions. Links: Eigenvalues and eigenspaces · Invariant subspace · Direct sum · Jordan canonical form · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Jordan / minimal poly

title: Generalized MVT
text: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem Let a<b, and let f,g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Then some c\in(a,b) satisfies f'(c)(g(b)-g(a))=g'(c)(f(b)-f(a)). Proof: apply Rolle's Theorem to h(x)=(g(b)-g(a))f(x)-(f(b)-f(a))g(x),\qquad h(a)=h(b). For g(x)=x, this becomes MVT. If g'\ne0 everywhere on (a,b), Rolle also gives g(b)\ne g(a), so division yields \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}. 原备注：写成相除的形式，需要注意两边分母都不是 0；相乘的版本没有这个要求。This theorem underlies proofs of L'Hôpital's rule (with that rule's additional hypotheses). Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder Supplement: one convenient sufficient hypothesis is f\in C^{n+1}([a,b]), a<b. Then some c\in(a,b) satisfies f(b)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(b-a)^k +\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(b-a)^{n+1}. For n=1: f(b)=f(a)+f'(a)(b-a)+\frac{f''(c)}2(b-a)^2. A finite Taylor formula is not yet equality with an infinite Taylor series; that requires the remainders to tend to zero. Fun fact: Lagrange is my math ancestor thanks to George. Links: MVT · Rolle's Theorem · Derivative · Taylor series · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 14

title: Goursat's theorem
text: Goursat If f is complex differentiable at every point of an open set U, then its integral around the boundary of every closed rectangle contained in U is zero. No continuity assumption on f' is needed. Proof idea: subdivide a rectangle into four congruent rectangles. Internal sides cancel, so one subrectangle has boundary integral of modulus at least one quarter of the original. Repeat to obtain nested rectangles R_n shrinking to a\in U, with \left|\int_{\partial R_n}f\,dz\right| \ge4^{-n}\left|\int_{\partial R_0}f\,dz\right|. Differentiability at a gives f(z)=f(a)+f'(a)(z-a)+\varepsilon(z)(z-a),\qquad \varepsilon(z)\to0. The affine part has a primitive, so its closed integral vanishes. Both the perimeter and diameter of R_n shrink by 2^{-n}; the ML estimate bounds the remaining integral by C\,4^{-n}\sup_{z\in R_n}|\varepsilon(z)|. Compare the two bounds and let n\to\infty. Complex differentiability already implies continuity of f. The local primitive construction then leads to Cauchy's formula, and hence to continuous derivatives of all orders and local power-series expansions. Role: the lecture notes first impose continuity of the derivative. Goursat shows that condition is redundant in the final definition of holomorphicity. Links: Holomorphic functions · ML estimate · Morera's theorem · Nested Closed Sets Theorem · Cauchy integral formula · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 34 · 132 notes, p. 35 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Gram-Schmidt
text: Start with an independent list (v_1,\ldots,v_n) in a real or complex inner-product space. Define successively u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\|u_k\|}. For k=1, the sum is empty. What the algorithm preserves The resulting list is orthonormal, and for every k, \operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_k)=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_k). Why it works: subtracting the projection makes u_k orthogonal to the previous e_j. If u_k=0, then v_k lies in the earlier span, contradicting independence. Normalization is therefore valid. Example: from v_1=(1,1), v_2=(1,0) in \mathbb R^2, e_1=\frac{(1,1)}{\sqrt2},\qquad u_2=(1/2,-1/2),\qquad e_2=\frac{(1,-1)}{\sqrt2}. For a dependent input, a residual may be zero; skip it rather than divide by zero. Every finite-dimensional inner-product space consequently has an orthonormal basis. If the residuals are kept unnormalized, the subtraction coefficients must be \langle v_k,u_j\rangle/\|u_j\|^2. Do not mix the normalized and unnormalized formulas. Links: Span and linear independence · Orthonormal basis · Orthogonal projection · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 12

title: Green's theorem and exact forms
text: Green's theorem Let D\subset\mathbb R^2 be a bounded region whose boundary consists of finitely many disjoint piecewise C^1 simple closed curves. If P,Q are C^1 on a neighborhood of \overline D, then \int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy =\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\,dy. The positive boundary orientation keeps D to the left: the outer boundary is counterclockwise, and boundaries of holes are clockwise. On an open set, a C^1 form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is closed if P_y=Q_x. It is exact if \omega=dF for a potential F, so F_x=P, F_y=Q. Exact forms are closed. On a simply connected domain, closed C^1 forms are exact. Exactness is equivalent to path independence and to zero integral around every piecewise smooth closed path in the domain. Counterexample: on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}, \omega=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} is closed, but its integral around the positive unit circle is 2\pi. Therefore it is not exact there. For a holomorphic f=u+iv, both u\,dx-v\,dy and v\,dx+u\,dy are closed by Cauchy-Riemann. This connects real line integrals to Cauchy's theorem. Links: Domains and simple connectedness · Harmonic conjugates · Contour integrals · Cauchy's theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 17 · 132 notes, p. 18 · 132 notes, p. 26 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Harmonic conjugates
text: Let u be real harmonic on a domain D. Harmonic conjugate A real function v is a harmonic conjugate of u if u+iv is holomorphic, equivalently v_x=-u_y,\qquad v_y=u_x. The form \omega=-u_y\,dx+u_x\,dy is closed because -u_{yy}=u_{xx}. On a simply connected domain, it is exact, so v(z)=v(z_0)+\int_{z_0}^{z}\omega is well-defined and is a harmonic conjugate. Every harmonic function therefore has conjugates locally, and has one globally if the domain is simply connected. Any two global conjugates on a domain differ by a real constant. Example: for u(x,y)=xy, integrate v_x=-x, v_y=y: v(x,y)=\frac{y^2-x^2}{2}+C,\qquad u+iv=-\frac{i}{2}z^2+iC. Boundary: u(z)=\log|z| is harmonic on \mathbb C\setminus\{0\}, but its conjugate form has integral 2\pi around the unit circle. A global conjugate would make this integral zero. Locally the conjugate is a branch of the argument. Links: Harmonic functions · Green's theorem and exact forms · Domains and simple connectedness · Branches of logarithms and powers · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 15 · 132 notes, p. 17 · 132 notes, p. 18 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Harmonic functions
text: Harmonicity A real-valued function u on an open set U\subseteq\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb R^2 is harmonic if u\in C^2(U) and \Delta u=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0. If f=u+iv is holomorphic, both u and v are harmonic. Indeed, holomorphic functions are smooth, and Cauchy-Riemann plus equality of mixed partials gives u_{xx}+u_{yy}=v_{yx}-v_{xy}=0. The argument for v is the same. Examples: x, y, x^2-y^2, xy are harmonic on the plane. The function \log|z| is harmonic on the punctured plane; |z|^2=x^2+y^2 is not, since its Laplacian is 4. Linear combinations of harmonic functions are harmonic. A complex-valued function is called harmonic when both its real and imaginary parts are harmonic; this does not imply it is holomorphic. For example, \overline z is complex harmonic but nowhere holomorphic. Boundary: two harmonic functions u,v need not make u+iv holomorphic. The pair must also satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations; this is the role of a harmonic conjugate. Links: Cauchy-Riemann equations · Harmonic conjugates · Mean value property · Maximum principle for harmonic functions · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 15 · 132 notes, p. 19 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Holomorphic functions
text: Let U\subseteq\mathbb C be open and a\in U. Complex derivative f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}h, if the limit exists for complex increments h\ne0. Equivalently, f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+o(|h|). Complex differentiability implies continuity, and the usual sum, product, quotient and chain rules hold where their expressions are defined. A function is holomorphic on U if it is complex differentiable at every point of U; it is entire if U=\mathbb C. By Goursat and Cauchy's formula, it then has continuous derivatives of all orders and is locally a convergent power series. In one complex variable, analytic and holomorphic therefore agree. Examples: polynomials and e^z are entire; rational functions are holomorphic away from denominator zeros. The function \overline z is nowhere complex differentiable: real increments give quotient 1, imaginary increments give -1. Boundary: |z|^2 is complex differentiable at 0, with derivative 0, but is holomorphic on no neighborhood of 0. On a domain, f'\equiv0 implies f is constant: its real and imaginary gradients vanish, and connect points by polygonal paths. Connectedness is needed to obtain one constant on the whole set. Links: Cauchy-Riemann equations · Goursat's theorem · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Derivative · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 8 · 132 notes, p. 9 · 132 notes, p. 11 · 132 notes, p. 12 · 132 notes, p. 34 · 132 summary, p. 1 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Holomorphic functions at infinity
text: Suppose f is holomorphic on |z|R for some R0. Coordinate at infinity The function is holomorphic at infinity if g(w)=f(1/w), initially defined for 0<|w|<1/R, extends holomorphically to w=0. Then f(\infty)=g(0)=\lim_{z\to\infty}f(z) is finite, and for all sufficiently large |z|, f(z)=b_0+\frac{b_1}{z}+\frac{b_2}{z^2}+\cdots. The inverse-power series is obtained from the Taylor series of g and converges uniformly on compact subsets of its exterior region. Local boundedness for sufficiently large |z| is an equivalent criterion, by the removable singularity theorem applied to g. Classification at infinity is also made through g: - f(z)=1/z is holomorphic at infinity, with value 0; - f(z)=z^m, m\ge1, has a pole of order m at infinity; - f(z)=e^z has an essential singularity at infinity, since e^{1/w} has infinitely many negative Laurent powers at 0. Boundary: holomorphic on an exterior region does not already mean holomorphic at infinity. A finite limit is required for a complex-valued holomorphic extension in this coordinate. Links: Riemann sphere · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Laurent series · Isolated singularities · Removable singularity theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 47 · 132 notes, p. 48 · 132 notes, p. 51

title: Identity theorem
text: Identity theorem Let f,g be holomorphic on a domain D. If the set \{z\in D:f(z)=g(z)\} has a limit point in D, then f\equiv g on D. Equivalently, it is enough to have distinct points z_n\in D with z_n\to a\in D and f(z_n)=g(z_n) for every n. Proof: h=f-g is holomorphic. Continuity gives h(a)=0, and the zeros accumulating at a are not isolated. The isolated zeros theorem forces h\equiv0. In particular, agreement on a nonempty open subset forces agreement on the whole connected domain. Having the same derivatives of every order at one interior point also suffices, by Taylor expansion. Boundary: the limit point must lie inside the domain. On \mathbb C\setminus\{0\}, the nonzero holomorphic function f(z)=\sin(\pi/z) vanishes at z=1/n, n\ge1, but these points accumulate at the excluded point 0. Connectedness also matters: agreement on one component says nothing about a different component. A repeated sequence at one point does not supply a limit point of distinct zeros. Links: Zeros of holomorphic functions · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Connectedness · Essential singularities · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 46 · 132 notes, p. 47 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Inner product
text: Let V be over \mathbb F=\mathbb R or \mathbb C. Convention: linear in the first argument An inner product \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F satisfies \langle ax+by,z\rangle=a\langle x,z\rangle+b\langle y,z\rangle, \langle x,y\rangle=\overline{\langle y,x\rangle}, \langle x,x\rangle\ge0,\qquad\langle x,x\rangle=0\iff x=0. Thus the second argument is conjugate-linear: \langle x,ay+bz\rangle=\overline a\langle x,y\rangle+\overline b\langle x,z\rangle. This agrees with the convention already used in L2 space. Examples: \langle x,y\rangle=\sum_jx_j\overline{y_j}\quad\text{on }\mathbb C^n, \langle f,g\rangle=\int_a^bf(t)\overline{g(t)}\,dt\quad\text{on }C([a,b],\mathbb C),\ a<b. The induced norm and metric are \|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle},\qquad d(x,y)=\|x-y\|. Their triangle inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Orthogonality means \langle x,y\rangle=0. Positive definiteness includes \langle0,0\rangle=0; “strictly positive for every vector” would be incorrect. Not every norm comes from an inner product: such norms must satisfy the parallelogram identity. Links: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality · Metric space · Orthogonal complement · L2 space · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 8 · 115A PDF, p. 9

title: Integral test
text: Theorem If f:[1,\infty)\to[0,\infty) is continuous and nonincreasing, then \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f(n)<\infty\iff\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx<\infty. Comparison by rectangles: for N\ge1, \int_1^{N+1}f(x)\,dx\le\sum_{n=1}^{N}f(n) \le f(1)+\int_1^N f(x)\,dx. Application: \sum1/n^p converges iff p1. For p0, apply the test to x^{-p}; for p\le0, the terms do not tend to 0. The monotonicity hypothesis is essential to this rectangle comparison; positivity and continuity alone are insufficient. Links: Partial sums · Comparison test · Riemann integral · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 10 · 131A PDF, p. 11

title: Interior, closure, boundary
text: Let E\subseteq X in a metric space (X,d); all complements and balls are relative to X. Definitions E^\circ=\{x\in E:\exists r0,\ B_X(x,r)\subseteq E\}, \overline E=\{x\in X:\forall r0,\ B_X(x,r)\cap E\ne\varnothing\}, \partial E=\overline E\setminus E^\circ. \overline E is also the intersection of all closed subsets of X containing E. A boundary point has every ball meeting both E and X\setminus E. Identities - E open \iff E=E^\circ. - E closed \iff E=\overline E. - \partial E=\overline E\cap\overline{X\setminus E}, hence the boundary is closed. - \overline E=E^\circ\cup\partial E (disjoint union). Example in \mathbb R: for E=(0,1], E^\circ=(0,1), \overline E=[0,1], \partial E=\{0,1\}. Links: Open & closed · Metric space · Compact set · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 7

title: Invariant subspace
text: Let T:V\to V be linear. A subspace W is T-invariant if T(W)\subseteq W. This allows both a restriction T|_W:W\to W and a quotient operator \overline T:V/W\to V/W,\qquad\overline T(v+W)=Tv+W. If v-u\in W, invariance ensures Tv-Tu\in W. Conversely, this formula is well-defined only if T(W)\subseteq W. In finite dimension, extend a basis of W to a basis of V. Then [T]=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&B\end{pmatrix}, where A represents T|_W and B represents \overline T in the corresponding quotient basis. Hence \chi_T(t)=\chi_{T|_W}(t)\chi_{\overline T}(t). The upper-right block need not vanish. An invariant subspace need not have an invariant complement: for T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad W=\operatorname{span}(1,0), there is no second invariant line complementary to W. Examples: eigenspaces, generalized eigenspaces and cyclic subspaces are invariant. For self-adjoint T, invariance of W also implies invariance of W^\perp. Links: Quotient space · Cyclic subspace · Generalized eigenspace · Spectral theorem · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Dual / Quotient

title: Isolated singularities
text: Let f be holomorphic on a punctured disk 0<|z-a|<R. The excluded point a is an isolated singularity; classify it using the Laurent expansion on that punctured disk. | Type | Negative Laurent coefficients | Equivalent local description | |---|---|---| | Removable | All vanish | f extends holomorphically across a | | Pole of order m\ge1 | Finitely many nonzero; lowest power is -m | f(z)=(z-a)^{-m}g(z), with g holomorphic and g(a)\ne0 | | Essential | Infinitely many nonzero | Neither removable nor a pole | The negative-power sum is the principal part. A pole satisfies |f(z)|\to\infty as z\to a; conversely, this limit characterizes a pole among isolated singularities. Examples at 0: \frac{\sin z}{z}\text{ is removable},\qquad \frac1{z^2}\text{ has a pole of order }2,\qquad e^{1/z}\text{ is essential}. Boundary: the residue is only the coefficient of (z-a)^{-1}. Residue 0 does not imply removability: 1/z^2 is a counterexample. Classification also requires a full punctured neighborhood; a branch point such as 0 for a square-root branch is not an isolated singularity of a single-valued holomorphic function on a punctured disk. Links: Laurent series · Removable singularity theorem · Poles and meromorphic functions · Essential singularities · Residue · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 52 · 132 notes, p. 53 · 132 notes, p. 54 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Isomorphism
text: Definition An isomorphism T:V\to W is a bijective linear map. Write V\cong W when one exists. Its inverse is linear. Indeed, if T(u)=x and T(v)=y, then T(au+bv)=ax+by, so T^{-1}(ax+by)=aT^{-1}x+bT^{-1}y. The inverse identities have different domains: T^{-1}T=I_V,\qquad TT^{-1}=I_W. Having only a left or a right inverse does not generally imply both. For finite-dimensional spaces over the same field, V\cong W\iff\dim V=\dim W. Choose bases of equal length and map corresponding basis vectors to one another. Such an isomorphism need not be canonical. Examples: the coordinate map V\to\mathbb F^n and \mathcal P_m(\mathbb F)\cong\mathbb F^{m+1} via coefficients. The spaces have the same linear structure, but their elements need not be the same objects. Links: Linear map · Basis and dimension · Rank-nullity theorem · Quotient space · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 4

title: IVT
text: Theorem Let a<b and f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R be continuous. If \min\{f(a),f(b)\}\le y\le\max\{f(a),f(b)\}, then some x\in[a,b] satisfies f(x)=y. Connectedness formulation: a continuous real-valued map on an interval has interval image (a singleton is allowed). For [a,b], compactness additionally makes that image a closed bounded interval. Consequences - Every real polynomial of odd degree has a real root: values at sufficiently large positive and negative inputs have opposite signs. - If f is continuous and strictly monotone on [a,b], it is a bijection onto its image interval, with continuous inverse. - For a strictly monotone function on an interval, having an interval image rules out jump discontinuities and implies continuity. Links: Continuity · Connectedness · Compact set · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 12

title: Jordan canonical form
text: Existence over the chosen field For A\in M_n(\mathbb F), a Jordan form A=PJP^{-1} exists iff its characteristic polynomial splits over \mathbb F. Each block is J_r(\lambda)=\lambda I+N, where N has ones immediately above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. A chain (v_1,\ldots,v_r) satisfies (T-\lambda I)v_1=0,\qquad(T-\lambda I)v_j=v_{j-1}\quad(j\ge2), with v_1\ne0. Its vectors are independent: applying successive powers of T-\lambda I to a relation kills all but its last surviving coefficient. A basis made of such chains gives Jordan blocks. For an eigenvalue \lambda: - the sum of block sizes is its algebraic multiplicity; - the number of blocks is \dim E_\lambda; - the largest block size is the exponent of t-\lambda in m_T. Recovering sizes: set d_0=0 and d_k=\dim\ker(T-\lambda I)^k. Then d_k-d_{k-1}=\\{\lambda\text{-blocks of size at least }k\}. The successive differences determine the blocks uniquely, up to order. Example: a nilpotent operator on a five-dimensional space with (d_1,d_2,d_3)=(2,4,5) has blocks of sizes 3 and 2. Here the kernels have already filled the whole space at k=3. Without the dimension or a stabilization condition, these three values would not rule out a larger block. If N^3=0 but N^2\ne0, the largest block has size exactly 3; this alone does not determine all other blocks. Diagonalization is precisely the case where all Jordan blocks have size 1. Links: Generalized eigenspace · Minimal polynomial · Diagonalization · Cyclic subspace · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Jordan / minimal poly

title: Kernel and image
text: Let T:V\to W be linear. \ker T=\{v\in V:T(v)=0\},\qquad\operatorname{im}T=\{T(v):v\in V\}. Both are subspaces, of V and W respectively. Injectivity and surjectivity T\text{ injective}\iff\ker T=\{0\}, T\text{ surjective}\iff\operatorname{im}T=W. For injectivity, T(u)=T(v) is equivalent to T(u-v)=0. Solving T(x)=b: a solution exists iff b\in\operatorname{im}T. If x_0 is one solution, every solution is x_0+\ker T=\{x_0+z:z\in\ker T\}. Thus a nonhomogeneous solution set is generally an affine translate of the kernel. For A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F), \operatorname{im}A is its column space, \operatorname{rank}A=\dim\operatorname{im}A, and \operatorname{nullity}A=\dim\ker A. The quotient V/\ker T removes precisely the ambiguity among preimages; see Quotient space. Links: Subspace · Linear map · Rank-nullity theorem · Quotient space · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 3 · 115A PDF, p. 8

title: L2 space
text: Course setting: continuous periodic functions The source notes work with f,g\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), where \mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z. Define \langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx, \|f\|_2=\left(\int_0^1|f|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad d_2(f,g)=\|f-g\|_2. The inner product is linear in its first argument. Continuity ensures positive definiteness: if a continuous f is nonzero at a point, |f| stays positive on a small interval, so \int|f|^20. Cauchy–Schwarz from Riemann integral yields |\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2 and the triangle inequality. Comparison with the sup norm (interval length 1): \|f-g\|_2\le\|f-g\|_\infty. Uniform convergence implies L^2 convergence. The converse fails: narrow continuous spikes can have height 1 but area tending to 0. For example, on [0,1] periodically extended, f_n(x)=\max\{1-n|x-1/2|,0\}\quad(n\ge2) has \|f_n\|_\infty=1 and \|f_n\|_2^2=2/(3n)\to0. Terminology boundary The full Lebesgue space L^2(\mathbb T) consists of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality almost everywhere. Without this identification, changing one point gives distance 0 between distinct functions. It is a complete space; C(\mathbb T) equipped with \|\cdot\|_2 is not complete. The existing Fourier cards state their results for the course's continuous-periodic setting; building the full Lebesgue theory is outside this review.
