title: Laurent series
text: Laurent expansion If f is holomorphic on A=\{z:r<|z-a|<R\}, with 0\le r<R\le\infty, then it has a unique expansion f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}c_n(z-a)^n, where, for any r<\rho<R, c_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|w-a|=\rho}\frac{f(w)}{(w-a)^{n+1}}\,dw\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z). Each coefficient circle is counterclockwise. The two one-sided sums converge absolutely at each point of A and uniformly on every smaller closed annulus. The nonnegative powers extend holomorphically to |z-a|<R. The negative powers extend holomorphically to |z-a|r and vanish at infinity. This normalization makes the decomposition unique. Proof route: apply Cauchy's formula between an inner and an outer circle. Expand each kernel geometrically in the appropriate ratio. Uniform convergence allows integration term by term; circle integrals of powers isolate each coefficient. Example from the notes: f(z)=\frac1{(z-1)(z-2)}=\frac1{z-2}-\frac1{z-1}. About 0, the expansions depend on the annulus: \begin{aligned} 0<|z|<1:&\quad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(1-2^{-n-1}\right)z^n,\\ 1<|z|<2:&\quad-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{2^{n+1}}-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^{-n},\\ 2<|z|:&\quad\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(2^n-1)z^{-n-1}. \end{aligned} Boundary: coefficients are unique for a fixed annulus, not across different annuli. The negative powers in the middle expansion do not make 0 a singularity of f: that expansion does not hold arbitrarily close to 0. Links: Complex power series · Cauchy integral formula · Holomorphic functions at infinity · Isolated singularities · Residue · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 48 · 132 notes, p. 49 · 132 notes, p. 50 · 132 notes, p. 51 · 132 notes, p. 52 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: limsup & liminf
text: For a real sequence (s_n), take sup/inf in [-\infty,+\infty]: \limsup_{n\to\infty}s_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{m\ge n}s_m=\inf_n\sup_{m\ge n}s_m, \liminf_{n\to\infty}s_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{m\ge n}s_m=\sup_n\inf_{m\ge n}s_m. Tail suprema decrease and tail infima increase, so both extended-real limits always exist. Finite convergence criterion For L\in\mathbb R, s_n\to L\iff\liminf s_n=\limsup s_n=L. Equality at +\infty or -\infty means an infinite limit, not convergence in \mathbb R. Subsequential limits For a bounded real sequence, let \mathcal S be its finite subsequential limits. Then \varnothing\ne\mathcal S,\qquad\min\mathcal S=\liminf s_n,\qquad\max\mathcal S=\limsup s_n. Without boundedness, finite subsequential limits can miss escape to infinity; see Subsequence. Example: s_n=(-1)^n gives \mathcal S=\{-1,1\}, \liminf=-1, \limsup=1. Links: Sup & inf · Subsequence · Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem · Root test · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 3 · 131A PDF, p. 4

title: Linear map
text: Let V,W be vector spaces over the same field \mathbb F. Definition T:V\to W is linear if T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)\quad(a,b\in\mathbb F,\ u,v\in V). Every linear map sends 0 to 0 and preserves finite linear combinations. An operator is a linear map T:V\to V. Basis principle: assigning arbitrary images T(v_j)=w_j to a basis of V determines a unique linear map: T\left(\sum_ja_jv_j\right)=\sum_ja_jw_j. This is why the columns of a matrix record basis-vector images. Examples: differentiation on polynomials, evaluation f\mapsto f(a), and integration f\mapsto\int_a^bf on C([a,b],\mathbb R). Counterexamples: a nonzero translation is not linear. Complex conjugation is \mathbb R-linear but not \mathbb C-linear. Linearity alone does not imply continuity in infinite-dimensional normed spaces. For example, differentiation on polynomials with the sup norm on [0,1] is unbounded: \|x^n\|_\infty=1 but \|(x^n)'\|_\infty=n. Links: Kernel and image · Matrix representation · Riemann integral · Spaces of functions · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 3

title: Liouville's theorem
text: Liouville A bounded entire function is constant. Proof: if |f|\le M on all of \mathbb C, Cauchy estimates give |f'(a)|\le\frac{M}{r} for every a\in\mathbb C and every r0. Let r\to\infty, then use f'\equiv0 on the connected plane. Consequences: - There is no holomorphic bijection from \mathbb C onto the unit disk: such a map would be bounded and therefore constant. - A nonconstant entire function has dense image in \mathbb C. If its image missed a disk D(w,\varepsilon), then 1/(f-w) would be bounded and entire, forcing f to be constant. Boundary: boundedness on a proper domain is insufficient; f(z)=z is bounded and nonconstant on the unit disk. Dense image also does not mean surjectivity: e^z omits 0. Links: Cauchy estimates · Holomorphic functions · Fundamental theorem of algebra · Essential singularities · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 32 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Lipschitz continuity
text: Definition A map f:(X,d_X)\to(Y,d_Y) is Lipschitz if some finite L\ge0 satisfies d_Y(f(x),f(y))\le Ld_X(x,y)\quad\forall x,y\in X. \text{Lipschitz}\implies\text{uniformly continuous}\implies\text{continuous}. Proof of first arrow: if L0, choose \delta=\varepsilon/L. If L=0, the map is constant (on a nonempty domain) and any positive \delta works. Converses fail - f(x)=\sqrt x on [0,1] is uniformly continuous by Heine–Cantor, but |f(x)-f(0)|/|x|=1/\sqrt x\to\infty. - f(x)=1/x on (0,1) is continuous but not uniformly continuous; see Continuity. Practical sufficient condition: if f is differentiable on an open interval I and |f'|\le L there, MVT gives |f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y| for x,y\in I. Include interval endpoints when f extends continuously to them. Links: Uniform continuity · Continuity in metric spaces · MVT · 131B Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Local extrema
text: Definition For f:D\to\mathbb R, x_0\in D is a local maximum point if \exists r0\ \forall x\in D\cap(x_0-r,x_0+r):\ f(x)\le f(x_0). Reverse the inequality for a local minimum. Fermat's theorem If x_0 is an interior point of D, f is differentiable at x_0, and x_0 is a local max/min, then f'(x_0)=0. Proof at a maximum: right-hand difference quotients are \le0, left-hand ones \ge0. Their common limit must be 0. Hypotheses and converse - f'(x_0)=0 is necessary under the theorem's hypotheses, but not sufficient: x^3 at 0. - Endpoints need not have zero derivative: f(x)=x has extrema at 0,1 on [0,1]. - A local extremum need not be differentiable: |x| at 0. Links: Derivative · Rolle's Theorem · MVT · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 14

title: Locally uniform convergence
text: Uniform on compact subsets Functions f_n on an open set U converge locally uniformly to f if \sup_{z\in K}|f_n(z)-f(z)|\to0 for every compact K\subset U. The lecture calls this normal convergence of a sequence. Here that term means compact uniform convergence; for series, some texts use normal convergence for the stronger condition of locally summable sup norms. Example: z^n\to0 locally uniformly on \mathbb D, since \sup_{|z|\le r}|z^n|=r^n\to0 for r<1. It does not converge uniformly on the whole disk, where the supremum is always 1. Holomorphic limit theorem If each f_n is holomorphic on U and f_n\to f locally uniformly, then f is holomorphic and f_n^{(m)}\to f^{(m)} locally uniformly for every m\ge1. Use Morera for holomorphicity. For derivatives, choose 0<r<s with \overline{D(a,s)}\subset U. Cauchy's formula gives \sup_{|z-a|\le r}|f_n^{(m)}(z)-f^{(m)}(z)| \le\frac{m!s}{(s-r)^{m+1}} \sup_{|w-a|=s}|f_n(w)-f(w)|. Cover a compact set by finitely many smaller disks. Boundary: in real analysis, uniform convergence of differentiable functions alone does not ensure convergence of their derivatives. Here holomorphicity and the room for a surrounding contour supply the stronger conclusion. Links: Uniform convergence · Uniform convergence theorems · Morera's theorem · Cauchy integral formula · Weierstrass M-test · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 36 · 132 notes, p. 37 · 132 notes, p. 38 · 132 notes, p. 39 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Matrix representation
text: Let T:V\to W be linear, with ordered bases \beta=(v_1,\ldots,v_n) and \gamma=(w_1,\ldots,w_m). Columns are images [T]_\beta^\gamma=\begin{bmatrix}[T(v_1)]_\gamma&\cdots&[T(v_n)]_\gamma\end{bmatrix}\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F). [T(v)]_\gamma=[T]_\beta^\gamma[v]_\beta. There are n columns, one per input basis vector, and m rows, one per output coordinate. “用输出的基，凑出输入基向量的像。” If S:W\to U and \delta is a basis of U, then [S\circ T]_\beta^\delta=[S]_\gamma^\delta[T]_\beta^\gamma. The middle basis must agree for ordinary matrix multiplication to describe composition. Example: for D:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)\to\mathcal P_1(\mathbb R), using (1,x,x^2) and (1,x), [D]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}. A matrix describes a map and a choice of bases. Changing the bases changes the matrix, not the underlying map. Links: Linear map · Basis and dimension · Change of basis and similarity · Rank-nullity theorem · 115A · Möbius transformations Source: 115A PDF, p. 4 · 115A PDF, p. 5

title: Maximum modulus principle
text: Maximum modulus If f is holomorphic and nonconstant on a domain D, then |f| has no local maximum in D. Proof idea: suppose |f| has a local maximum at a. If f(a)=0, then f=0 nearby. Otherwise choose \lambda with |\lambda|=1 and \lambda f(a)=|f(a)|. Near a, \operatorname{Re}(\lambda f(z))\le|f(z)|\le|f(a)|. The real part is harmonic, so its maximum principle forces it to be constant. Cauchy-Riemann then forces f to be constant; connectedness propagates the conclusion. If D is bounded and f\in C(\overline D) is holomorphic in D, then \max_{\overline D}|f|=\max_{\partial D}|f|. Minimum modulus: if f is zero-free on D, apply the maximum principle to 1/f. A nonconstant zero-free holomorphic function has no interior local minimum of its modulus. The corresponding boundary minimum statement requires f continuous and zero-free on \overline D. Boundary: f(z)=z has an interior minimum of |f| at its zero. Holomorphicity of f does not mean |f| is harmonic; the proof uses a rotated real part or 1/f. Links: Maximum principle for harmonic functions · Holomorphic functions · Schwarz lemma · Identity theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 19 · 132 notes, p. 20 · 132 notes, p. 43 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Maximum principle for harmonic functions
text: Strong maximum and minimum principles A nonconstant real harmonic function on a domain has no interior local maximum or minimum. Proof route: the mean value property forces equality on a small disk around a maximizing point. Harmonic functions have local holomorphic representations, so they are real analytic; constancy propagates across the connected domain. For a global maximum, one can instead show directly that the maximum set is both open and closed. Apply the result to -u for minima. If D is bounded and u\in C(\overline D) is real harmonic in D, then \max_{\overline D}u=\max_{\partial D}u,\qquad \min_{\overline D}u=\min_{\partial D}u. Compactness guarantees the extrema exist; an interior extremum forces constancy. Complex harmonic version: if h is complex harmonic and |h| has an interior maximum, rotate h so that its value there is real and nonnegative. Apply the real maximum principle to the real part and use \operatorname{Re}h\le|h|. This forces h to be constant. Consequence: two real harmonic functions continuous on the closure of a bounded domain and agreeing on its boundary agree everywhere. Apply the maximum and minimum principles to their difference. Boundary: boundedness matters for the boundary conclusion. On the upper half-plane, u(x,y)=y vanishes on the boundary but is positive inside. Also |h| need not itself be harmonic. Links: Mean value property · Harmonic conjugates · Maximum modulus principle · Compact set · Identity theorem · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 19 · 132 notes, p. 20 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Mean value property
text: Harmonic mean value If u is harmonic on an open set containing \overline{D(a,r)}, then u(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(a+re^{i\theta})\,d\theta. The same identity holds componentwise for complex-valued harmonic functions, hence for holomorphic functions. Proof idea: for 0<s\le r, let A(s)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(a+se^{i\theta})\,d\theta. Differentiate under the integral. Green's theorem gives 2\pi s A'(s)=\int_{\partial D(a,s)}(-u_y\,dx+u_x\,dy) =\iint_{D(a,s)}\Delta u\,dx\,dy=0. Thus A(s) is constant; continuity and s\downarrow0 give A(s)=u(a). Integrating the circle formula in the radius also gives the disk average u(a)=\frac1{\pi r^2}\iint_{D(a,r)}u(x,y)\,dx\,dy. Use: if u\le M near a and u(a)=M, the average can equal M only if u=M on each sufficiently small circle. This is the local step behind the maximum principle. Links: Harmonic functions · Green's theorem and exact forms · Maximum principle for harmonic functions · Cauchy integral formula · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 18 · 132 notes, p. 19 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Metric space
text: Definition A metric space (X,d) has a finite-valued distance d:X\times X\to[0,\infty) satisfying d(x,y)=0\iff x=y,\qquad d(x,y)=d(y,x), d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). Open ball: B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}, for r0. | Space | Metric | Required domain | |---|---|---| | \mathbb R | \lvert x-y\rvert | Real numbers | | \mathbb R^d | \sqrt{\sum_j(x_j-y_j)^2} | Finite-dimensional Euclidean space | | B(S,\mathbb R) | \sup_{x\in S}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert | Bounded functions on a nonempty set S | | C(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,\mathbb C) | \left(\int_0^1\lvert f-g\rvert^2\right)^{1/2} | Continuous periodic functions; see L2 space | For arbitrary functions the sup can be infinite. For arbitrary integrable functions, L^2 distance can be zero between functions that differ at individual points; continuity or an almost-everywhere equivalence relation resolves this. What generalizes: the definitions of convergence, Cauchy sequences, open/closed sets, continuity, and compactness use d in place of Euclidean distance. What needs extra hypotheses: - Cauchy \Rightarrow convergent requires completeness. - Closed and bounded \Rightarrow compact is the Euclidean Heine–Borel theorem, not a general metric-space fact. Counterexample: an infinite discrete space, d(x,y)=1 for x\ne y, is bounded and complete but not compact: its singleton open cover has no finite subcover. Links: Completeness of a metric space · Open & closed · Continuity in metric spaces · Compactness and continuity · Spaces of functions · 131B · Inner product Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Minimal polynomial
text: Let T\in\mathcal L(V), where V\ne\{0\} is finite-dimensional over \mathbb F. Definition The minimal polynomial m_T is the monic polynomial of smallest degree such that m_T(T)=0. It exists by Cayley-Hamilton theorem. Polynomial division shows that every annihilating polynomial is divisible by m_T: if p=qm_T+r and p(T)=0, then r(T)=0, forcing r=0 by minimality. In particular, m_T\mid\chi_T. The two polynomials have the same irreducible factors, but generally different multiplicities. Diagonalization criterion T is diagonalizable over \mathbb F iff m_T(t)=\prod_{j=1}^r(t-\lambda_j) for distinct \lambda_j\in\mathbb F. For the reverse implication, Lagrange polynomials p_j(t)=\prod_{i\ne j}\frac{t-\lambda_i}{\lambda_j-\lambda_i} give projections p_j(T) onto the eigenspaces, with \sum_jp_j(T)=I. Examples: m_I=t-1, while \chi_{I_n}=(t-1)^n. A nontrivial 2\times2 Jordan block at 1 has m_T=(t-1)^2. A real 90^\circ rotation has m_T=t^2+1: no repeated roots, but no splitting over \mathbb R, hence no real diagonalization. When Jordan form exists, the exponent of t-\lambda in m_T is the size of the largest block for \lambda. Links: Cayley-Hamilton theorem · Diagonalization · Jordan canonical form · Cyclic subspace · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Jordan / minimal poly

title: ML estimate
text: Length estimate If \gamma is piecewise C^1, f is continuous on its image, |f|\le M there and L=L(\gamma), then \left|\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz\right| \le\int_\gamma|f(z)|\,|dz|\le ML. Proof: apply the triangle inequality to \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt. Sharp example: on |z|=R traversed once counterclockwise, f(z)=1/z has M=1/R, L=2\pi R, and integral 2\pi i. Equality holds in the estimate. If continuous f_n\to f uniformly on a fixed path image, then \left|\int_\gamma f_n\,dz-\int_\gamma f\,dz\right| \le L(\gamma)\sup_{z\in\gamma}|f_n(z)-f(z)|\to0. This is the contour version of uniform convergence allowing integration through a limit. Boundary: the path and the bound must match. A holomorphic logarithm branch cannot be chosen continuously around an entire circle enclosing 0. An expression involving principal \operatorname{Log} on that circle needs a cut and an explicit piecewise interpretation; do not treat it as one continuous branch along a closed loop. Links: Contour integrals · Uniform convergence · Locally uniform convergence · Branches of logarithms and powers · Real integrals by residues · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 22 · 132 notes, p. 23 · 132 notes, p. 24 · 132 notes, p. 37 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Möbius transformations
text:
Fractional linear transformation T(z)= rac{az+b}{cz+d},\qquad a,b,c,d\in\mathbb C,\quad ad-bc
e0. For c
e0, set T(-d/c)=\infty and T(\infty)=a/c. For c=0, T is affine and T(\infty)=\infty. This makes T a bijection of \widehat{\mathbb C}, with inverse T^{-1}(w)= rac{dw-b}{-cw+a}. The matrix  egin{pmatrix}a&b\c&d\end{pmatrix} determines T up to multiplication by a nonzero scalar. Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication in the same order. At finite non-pole points, T'(z)= rac{ad-bc}{(cz+d)^2}
e0. Three-point theorem: for any ordered triple of distinct sphere points (z_1,z_2,z_3) and another such triple (w_1,w_2,w_3), there is exactly one Möbius map sending each z_j to w_j. For finite distinct z_j, the map S(z)= rac{(z-z_1)(z_2-z_3)}{(z-z_3)(z_2-z_1)} sends them to (0,1,\infty). Use limits if one point is infinity, then compose with the inverse of the corresponding map for the target triple. Examples: (z-i)/(z+i) sends (0,i,\infty) to (-1,0,1). If |a|<1, then \phi_a(z)= rac{z-a}{1-\overline a z},\qquad 1-|\phi_a(z)|^2= rac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\overline a z|^2}. Thus \phi_a maps the unit disk to itself and its boundary to itself; its inverse is (w+a)/(1+\overline a w). title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
text: Theorem (real sequences) Nondecreasing and bounded above \implies x_n\to\sup_n x_n. Nonincreasing and bounded below \implies x_n\to\inf_n x_n. Proof (nondecreasing): put L=\sup_n x_n. Given \varepsilon0, choose N with L-\varepsilon<x_N. Then n\ge N\implies L-\varepsilon<x_N\le x_n\le L\implies |x_n-L|<\varepsilon. Unbounded case: nondecreasing and unbounded above \implies x_n\to+\infty; nonincreasing and unbounded below \implies x_n\to-\infty. Thus a monotone real sequence always has an extended-real limit. title: Morera's theorem
text: Morera Let f be continuous on an open set U. If \int_{\partial R}f(z)\,dz=0 for every closed rectangle R\subset U with sides parallel to the coordinate axes, then f is holomorphic on U. A standard equivalent version uses boundaries of all triangles contained in U. These are local tests; simple connectedness of U is not required. Proof idea: work in a small rectangle. Define F(z) by integrating f from a fixed point along horizontal and vertical segments. The zero-rectangle condition makes the two orders of travel agree. Continuity yields F_x=f,\qquad F_y=if. Thus F is holomorphic and F'=f. Cauchy's formula shows that the derivative of a holomorphic function is holomorphic, so f is holomorphic. Use for limits: if holomorphic f_n converge uniformly on compact subsets of U, the limit is continuous. For a rectangle compactly contained in U, the ML estimate lets the limit pass through the boundary integral, giving zero; apply Morera. Boundary: continuity is a hypothesis, not a consequence of the integral condition alone. The function equal to 1 at one point and 0 elsewhere has zero integrals around rectangle boundaries but is not continuous at that point. title: MVT
text: Theorem Let a<b, f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Then \exists c\in(a,b):\quad f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. Geometric meaning: some tangent is parallel to the secant from a to b. Proof: set g(x)=f(x)-\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x-a). Then g(a)=g(b)=f(a). By Rolle's Theorem, 0=g'(c)=f'(c)-\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. title: Nested Closed Sets Theorem
text: Theorem Let F_1\supseteq F_2\supseteq\cdots be nonempty closed subsets of \mathbb R^d, with F_1 bounded. Then \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}F_n\ne\varnothing. Proof: choose x_n\in F_n\subseteq F_1. By Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem, x_{n_k}\to x. For each fixed m, eventually n_k\ge m, so x_{n_k}\in F_m; closedness gives x\in F_m. Thus x\in\bigcap_mF_m. Hypotheses matter - Without boundedness: F_n=[n,\infty) have empty intersection. - Without closedness: F_n=(0,1/n) have empty intersection. Metric-space version: a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets has nonempty intersection. More generally, use nonempty closed subsets of one fixed compact set. “Closed and bounded” alone does not supply compactness in an arbitrary metric space. title: Normal and self-adjoint operators
text: Let T be an operator on a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space. T\text{ self-adjoint}\iff T=T^,\qquad T\text{ normal}\iff TT^=T^T. Every self-adjoint operator is normal. In orthonormal coordinates, self-adjoint matrices are real symmetric or complex Hermitian. Normality and eigenvectors If T is normal, then Tx=\lambda x\iff T^x=\overline\lambda x. Proof idea: for normal S, \|Sx\|=\|S^x\|. Apply this to the normal operator S=T-\lambda I. Its kernel equals that of S^. If Tx=\lambda x and Ty=\mu y with \lambda\ne\mu, then normality gives \lambda\langle x,y\rangle=\langle Tx,y\rangle =\langle x,T^y\rangle=\mu\langle x,y\rangle, so x\perp y. A self-adjoint operator has real eigenvalues: \lambda\|x\|^2=\langle Tx,x\rangle is real for an eigenvector x. Counterexample to a converse: multiplication by i on \mathbb C is normal but not self-adjoint. A real plane rotation is normal but need not have real eigenvectors. The field distinction is essential in the Spectral theorem. Links: Adjoint · Eigenvalues and eigenspaces · Spectral theorem · Unitary and orthogonal operators · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 15

title: Open & closed
text: Work in an ambient metric space (X,d); in 131A, X=\mathbb R or \mathbb R^d. Definitions U\subseteq X is open if \forall x\in U\ \exists r0:\ B_X(x,r)\subseteq U. F\subseteq X is closed if X\setminus F is open. Clopen means both; X and \varnothing are clopen. Sequential characterization F\text{ closed in }X\iff [x_n\in F,\ x_n\to x\text{ in }X\implies x\in F]. If X is complete, this also says every Cauchy sequence in F converges in F. Without completeness the Cauchy formulation fails: \mathbb Q is closed in itself but is not complete. Stability under unions and intersections | Operation | Open sets | Closed sets | |---|---|---| | Arbitrary union | Open | Not necessarily closed | | Finite union | Open | Closed | | Arbitrary intersection | Not necessarily open | Closed | | Finite intersection | Open | Closed | De Morgan's laws (complements in X): \left(\bigcup_\alpha E_\alpha\right)^c=\bigcap_\alpha E_\alpha^c, \qquad\left(\bigcap_\alpha E_\alpha\right)^c=\bigcup_\alpha E_\alpha^c. title: Operations on power series
text: Suppose f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n and g(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nz^n converge on |z|<R, with R0. On this common disk, f(z)+g(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}(a_n+b_n)z^n, f(z)g(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nz^n,\qquad c_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n}a_jb_{n-j}. Absolute convergence justifies the Cauchy product and rearrangement. If b_0\ne0, write g=b_0(1+B) with B(0)=0. On a sufficiently small disk, |B|<1, so \frac1g=\frac1{b_0}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-B)^k. Equivalently, if 1/g=\sum c_nz^n, then c_0=\frac1{b_0},\qquad c_n=-\frac1{b_0}\sum_{j=1}^{n}b_jc_{n-j}\quad(n\ge1). Example from the notes: near 0, \frac{e^z}{1+z} =\left(1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+O(z^4)\right) \left(1-z+z^2-z^3+O(z^4)\right) =1+\frac{z^2}{2}-\frac{z^3}{3}+O(z^4). The full Taylor series has radius 1, because -1 is a genuine pole. Boundary: g(0)\ne0 ensures a local reciprocal, not a zero-free original disk. The geometric expression requires |B(z)|<1 where it is used; the reciprocal may extend further by other means. title: Orthogonal complement
text: For any subset S of an inner-product space V, S^\perp=\{x\in V:\langle x,s\rangle=0\text{ for every }s\in S\}. It is always a subspace, even if S is not a subspace or is infinite. \{0\}^\perp=V,\qquad V^\perp=\{0\},\qquad S^\perp=(\operatorname{span}S)^\perp. Also S\subseteq(S^\perp)^\perp, and S\subseteq R implies R^\perp\subseteq S^\perp. Orthogonal decomposition If W\subseteq V is a finite-dimensional subspace, then V=W\oplus W^\perp. Every v has a unique decomposition v=w+z, with w\in W, z\in W^\perp. Choose an orthonormal basis of W and take w=\sum_j\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j. Then v-w is perpendicular to every basis vector. Uniqueness follows from W\cap W^\perp=\{0\}. If V is finite-dimensional, then \dim W^\perp=\dim V-\dim W,\qquad(S^\perp)^\perp=\operatorname{span}S. Do not apply the last identity to arbitrary infinite-dimensional spaces without further hypotheses. The definition of S^\perp itself needs no finite-dimensional assumption. Links: Inner product · Orthogonal projection · Orthonormal basis · Direct sum · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 10

title: Orthogonal projection
text: Let W be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner-product space V. Orthogonal projection P_Wv is the unique vector in W such that v-P_Wv\in W^\perp. For an orthonormal basis (e_1,\ldots,e_m) of W, P_Wv=\sum_{j=1}^m\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j. For an orthogonal basis of nonzero vectors (u_j), divide each coefficient by \|u_j\|^2 instead. A merely nonorthogonal basis does not permit either formula. Best approximation For every w\in W, \|v-w\|^2=\|v-P_Wv\|^2+\|P_Wv-w\|^2. The two terms are orthogonal. Hence P_Wv is the unique closest vector in W to v. P_W is linear and satisfies P_W^2=P_W, \operatorname{im}P_W=W, \ker P_W=W^\perp and \|P_Wv\|\le\|v\|. It is self-adjoint. Caution: idempotence alone does not mean orthogonal projection: P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^2=P,\quad P^{\mathsf T}\ne P. In finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, an operator is an orthogonal projection iff P^2=P and P^=P. Fourier partial sums are projections onto finite spans of exponentials. Their best-approximation property uses this same identity. Links: Orthogonal complement · Orthonormal basis · Adjoint · Fourier coefficients · Parseval identity · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 9 · 115A PDF, p. 10 · 115A PDF, p. 11 · 115B PDF, p. 1

title: Orthonormal basis
text: A list (e_1,\ldots,e_n) is orthonormal if \langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}. Every orthonormal list is independent: take the inner product of \sum a_je_j=0 with e_k to obtain a_k=0. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis If the list is a basis of V, then v=\sum_{j=1}^n\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j. The order of the inner-product arguments uses the convention “linear in the first argument.” For x=\sum a_je_j and y=\sum b_je_j, \langle x,y\rangle=\sum_ja_j\overline{b_j},\qquad \|x\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2. Thus orthonormal coordinates preserve both linear structure and the inner product. If the list does not span V, the sum gives the projection of v, not necessarily v itself; then \sum_j|\langle v,e_j\rangle|^2\le\|v\|^2. The finite identity is the starting point for Parseval identity. Passing to an infinite family requires convergence and completeness/density arguments, not just the finite coordinate calculation. Links: Inner product · Gram-Schmidt · Orthogonal projection · Parseval identity · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 11

title: Parseval identity
text: Let f\in C(\mathbb T,\mathbb C), \mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, and F_N=\sum_{|n|\le N}\widehat f(n)e_n. Finite orthogonal identities By orthonormality and projection, \|F_N\|_2^2=\sum_{|n|\le N}|\widehat f(n)|^2, \|f\|_2^2=\|F_N\|_2^2+\|f-F_N\|_2^2. In particular, \sum_{|n|\le N}|\widehat f(n)|^2\le\|f\|_2^2 (Bessel's inequality). Passing to the limit For \varepsilon0, Fourier theorem gives a trig polynomial P\in V_M with \|f-P\|_\infty<\varepsilon. For N\ge M, the projection minimizes L^2 error: \|f-F_N\|_2\le\|f-P\|_2\le\|f-P\|_\infty<\varepsilon. Therefore F_N\to f in L^2, and Parseval \int_0^1|f(x)|^2\,dx=\|f\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(n)|^2. Meaning: energy in the function equals energy in its Fourier coefficients. The argument uses L^2 convergence of F_N, not uniform convergence. Links: Fourier coefficients · L2 space · Fourier theorem · 131B · Orthonormal basis · Orthogonal projection Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Partial sums
text: Definition For a real sequence (a_n), put S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i. \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n=S\in\mathbb R\iff S_n\to S. If a_n\ge0, then (S_n) is nondecreasing. By Monotone Convergence Theorem, the series converges to a finite sum iff its partial sums are bounded above; otherwise S_n\to+\infty. Necessary, not sufficient \sum a_n\text{ converges}\implies a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\to0. The converse fails: \sum 1/n diverges. Links: Cauchy criterion for series · Absolute convergence · Monotone Convergence Theorem · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 8

title: Pointwise convergence
text: Definition For real-valued functions f_n,f on S, f_n\to f\text{ pointwise}\iff \forall x\in S\ \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists N=N(\varepsilon,x)\ \forall n\ge N: |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon. Fix x first: each point can converge at its own rate. Uniform convergence requires the same N(\varepsilon) for every x. Example: f_n(x)=x^n on [0,1] gives f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases} Every f_n is continuous; f is not. Moreover \sup_{[0,1]}|f_n-f|=1, so convergence is not uniform. Pointwise convergence alone does not preserve continuity, Riemann integrability, or differentiability. Any exchange of limits with integrals or derivatives needs an additional theorem and its hypotheses. Links: Uniform convergence · Uniform convergence theorems · Continuity · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 15

title: Poles and meromorphic functions
text: Pole A function holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood has a pole of order m\ge1 at a iff f(z)=\frac{g(z)}{(z-a)^m}, where g is holomorphic near a and g(a)\ne0. This is equivalent to 1/f having a zero of order m at a, after restricting to a smaller punctured disk and extending the reciprocal at a. It also implies |f(z)|\to\infty. Conversely, if |f(z)|\to\infty at an isolated singularity, then 1/f\to0 extends holomorphically. Its zero has finite order, so f has a pole. A function is meromorphic on a domain if it is holomorphic except at a discrete set of poles. These poles have no accumulation point inside the domain. Holomorphic functions are included as the case with no poles. If g,h are holomorphic, h is not identically zero on the domain, and removable points are filled in, then g/h is meromorphic. If their finite zero orders at a are m,n, respectively, cancellation gives a pole of order n-m when nm, and a removable point when n\le m. Example: (z^2-1)/(z-1) has a removable point at 1 with extension z+1, whereas 1/(z-1)^2 has a double pole. A zero of a written denominator need not survive cancellation. Links: Zeros of holomorphic functions · Isolated singularities · Removable singularity theorem · Residue · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 53 · 132 notes, p. 54 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Positive definite matrix
text: Let A=A^{\mathsf T}\in M_n(\mathbb R). - Positive definite: x^{\mathsf T}Ax0 for every x\ne0. - Positive semidefinite: x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge0 for every x; this includes positive definite matrices. - Indefinite: the form takes both positive and negative values. By the Spectral theorem, these correspond to all eigenvalues being positive, all being nonnegative, or having both signs. A singular positive semidefinite matrix additionally has a zero eigenvalue. Sylvester's criterion A real symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all its leading principal minors are positive: \Delta_k=\det A_{1:k,1:k}0\quad(k=1,\ldots,n). Proof idea: successive completion of squares gives pivots \Delta_k/\Delta_{k-1}, with \Delta_0=1. Positive pivots make the diagonal form positive; conversely, every leading principal restriction of a positive definite form is positive definite. The source's matrix \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix} has \Delta_1=2, \Delta_2=5, hence is positive definite. Replacing by \ge for leading minors does not characterize semidefiniteness: \operatorname{diag}(0,-1) has leading minors 0,0 but takes negative values. For positive semidefinite A, x^{\mathsf T}Ax=0 iff Ax=0. For indefinite forms this fails: x_1^2-x_2^2 vanishes on two lines, although its matrix is invertible. A quadratic form is not a linear map, so its zero set should not generally be called a kernel. Positive definite A defines an inner product \langle x,y\rangle_A=x^{\mathsf T}Ay on \mathbb R^n. Links: Quadratic form · Sylvester law of inertia · Inner product · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Quadratic form

title: Power series
text: For real x,c and real or complex coefficients, consider \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n. Radius of convergence R=\frac1{\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}},\qquad 1/0=+\infty,\quad1/(+\infty)=0. By Root test: - |x-c|<R: absolute convergence. - |x-c|R: divergence. - For 0<R<\infty, check each endpoint c-R,c+R separately. - At x=c, the series always converges to a_0, including when R=0. Inside the interval of convergence On |x-c|\le r<R, choose r<\rho<R (for r=0 the conclusion is immediate). Convergence at radius \rho bounds |a_n|\rho^n, giving a geometric majorant on radius r. The Weierstrass M-test yields uniform convergence. If R0, the sum f is continuous and f'(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}na_n(x-c)^{n-1}, \int_c^xf(t)\,dt=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{n+1}(x-c)^{n+1} \quad(|x-c|<R). The differentiated series has the same radius and converges uniformly on smaller closed intervals; apply Uniform convergence theorems. Uniform convergence of the original series alone would not justify differentiation. Links: Taylor series · limsup & liminf · Root test · Absolute convergence · Uniform convergence theorems · 131B · Complex power series Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Primitives and path independence
text: Primitive A primitive of f on an open set is a holomorphic function F satisfying F'=f. If F is a primitive and \gamma runs from a to b, then \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=F(b)-F(a). Use the chain rule for F\circ\gamma and the real fundamental theorem of calculus on each smooth segment. For continuous f on a domain D, the following are equivalent: - f has a primitive on D; - the integral of f depends only on the endpoints; - the integral is zero around every piecewise smooth closed path in D. For the reverse direction, fix z_0\in D and define F(z)=\int_{z_0}^{z}f(w)\,dw. Path independence makes this well-defined. On a small disk, compare values using a straight segment; continuity gives F'(z)=f(z). Two primitives on a domain differ by a constant. Existence theorem: every holomorphic function on a simply connected domain has a primitive, by Cauchy's theorem. Boundary: 1/z is holomorphic on the punctured plane but has no primitive there, since its unit-circle integral is 2\pi i. The function 1/z^2 does have the global primitive -1/z on that same domain. Links: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus · Cauchy's theorem · Domains and simple connectedness · Branches of logarithms and powers · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 24 · 132 notes, p. 25 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Quadratic form
text: A real quadratic form on \mathbb R^n can be written q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax,\qquad A=A^{\mathsf T}. Any matrix B gives the same quadratic form as its symmetric part (B+B^{\mathsf T})/2; the skew-symmetric part contributes zero. Cross terms are halved: the source's example q(x,y,z)=2x^2+3y^2-z^2+4xy-6xz+8yz has symmetric matrix A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2&-3\\2&3&4\\-3&4&-1\end{pmatrix}. Both a_{ij}x_ix_j and a_{ji}x_jx_i contribute to the same cross term. Changing coordinates If x=Py with P invertible, then q(x)=y^{\mathsf T}(P^{\mathsf T}AP)y. The matrix changes by congruence, not general similarity. By the real Spectral theorem, choose orthogonal Q with A=QDQ^{\mathsf T}. Setting y=Q^{\mathsf T}x gives q(x)=\lambda_1y_1^2+\cdots+\lambda_ny_n^2. The signs of the eigenvalues determine the possible signs of q. Completing the square: 2x^2+2xy+3y^2=2(x+y/2)^2+\tfrac52y^2. This also removes cross terms, but the coordinate change need not be orthogonal. The resulting coefficients need not be eigenvalues. Links: Spectral theorem · Sylvester law of inertia · Positive definite matrix · Change of basis and similarity · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Quadratic form

title: Quotient space
text: Let W be a subspace of V. The quotient space consists of cosets V/W=\{v+W:v\in V\},\qquad v+W=u+W\iff v-u\in W. Define (u+W)+(v+W)=(u+v)+W and a(v+W)=av+W. These are independent of the chosen representatives because W is a subspace. Quotient map \pi:V\to V/W,\qquad\pi(v)=v+W is linear and surjective, with \ker\pi=W. The zero vector of V/W is the coset W, not a single vector of V. If V is finite-dimensional, extend a basis of W to one of V. The cosets of the additional vectors form a basis of the quotient, so \dim(V/W)=\dim V-\dim W. First isomorphism theorem For a linear map T:V\to U, V/\ker T\cong\operatorname{im}T,\qquad v+\ker T\longmapsto Tv. The map is well-defined because equal cosets differ by a kernel vector; it is injective and surjective by construction. No finite-dimensional assumption is needed for this isomorphism. Example: if W is the horizontal axis in \mathbb R^2, a coset records only the vertical coordinate. A quotient identifies vectors; it is not automatically an orthogonal complement. Links: Kernel and image · Rank-nullity theorem · Direct sum · Invariant subspace · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Dual / Quotient

title: Rank-nullity theorem
text: Rank-nullity If T:V\to W is linear and \dim V=n<\infty, then \dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=n. There is no need for the whole codomain W to be finite-dimensional. Proof sketch: extend a basis (u_1,\ldots,u_k) of \ker T to a basis (u_1,\ldots,u_k,v_1,\ldots,v_{n-k}) of V. Then T(v_1),\ldots,T(v_{n-k}) span the image. A relation among them puts \sum a_jv_j in the kernel, forcing all a_j=0. For A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F), \operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{nullity}A=n, \operatorname{rank}A^{\mathsf T}+\operatorname{nullity}A^{\mathsf T}=m. The dimension on the right is the number of input coordinates. If \dim V=\dim W<\infty, then injective, surjective and invertible are equivalent for T:V\to W. Finite dimension of V alone is not enough when the codomain has a different dimension: x\mapsto(x,0) from \mathbb R to \mathbb R^2 is injective but not surjective. Links: Kernel and image · Basis and dimension · Isomorphism · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 4 · 115A PDF, p. 8

title: Ratio test
text: Theorem Assume a_n\ne0 for all sufficiently large n, and set r_n=|a_{n+1}/a_n|. - \limsup r_n<1: \sum a_n converges absolutely. - \liminf r_n1: \sum a_n diverges. - Otherwise this test is inconclusive. The conclusions follow from eventual geometric upper/lower bounds on |a_n|. Relation to Root test: \liminf r_n\le\liminf |a_n|^{1/n} \le\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}\le\limsup r_n. Thus a decisive ratio test implies a decisive root test. Converse fails: take a_{2k}=4^{-k}\ (k\ge1),\qquad a_{2k+1}=4^{-k}\ (k\ge0). Ratios alternate between 1 and 1/4, so \limsup r_n=1 is inconclusive; however |a_n|^{1/n}\to1/2, so the root test gives convergence. Links: limsup & liminf · Absolute convergence · Root test · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 9

title: Real integrals by residues
text: The source example evaluates, for real a, \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(ax)}{1+x^2}\,dx=\pi e^{-|a|}. The improper integral is absolutely convergent because the integrand is bounded in modulus by 1/(1+x^2). For a\ge0: take f(z)=\frac{e^{iaz}}{1+z^2} on the positively oriented upper half-disk of radius R1. Its boundary is the segment from -R to R, followed by the upper semicircle \Gamma_R from R to -R. The only enclosed pole is i, with residue e^{-a}/(2i), so \int_{-R}^{R}\frac{e^{iax}}{1+x^2}\,dx+\int_{\Gamma_R}f(z)\,dz=\pi e^{-a}. On the upper semicircle, |e^{iaz}|=e^{-a\operatorname{Im}z}\le1 and |1+z^2|\ge R^2-1. Therefore \left|\int_{\Gamma_R}f(z)\,dz\right| \le\frac{\pi R}{R^2-1}\longrightarrow0. Let R\to\infty and take real parts. The estimate also covers a=0; for a<0, use \cos(ax)=\cos(|a|x). Boundary: symmetry of the finite interval alone would give only a principal-value limit. Here absolute convergence makes it the ordinary improper integral. For other exponential contour integrals, choose the half-plane where the exponential decays and prove the closing arc tends to zero; residues alone do not establish that step. Links: Residue theorem · Residue · ML estimate · Riemann integral · Fourier coefficients · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 56 · 132 notes, p. 57

title: Removable singularity theorem
text: Riemann removable singularity theorem Suppose f is holomorphic on 0<|z-a|<R. If it is bounded on some smaller punctured neighborhood of a, then it extends holomorphically across a. For an isolated singularity, the following are equivalent: - it is removable; - f is bounded near a; - \lim_{z\to a}f(z) exists and is finite. The extension is unique, with its value at a equal to that limit. Proof by coefficients: if |f|\le M near a, then for a sufficiently small positive circle radius \rho and every k\ge1, |c_{-k}|=\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|z-a|=\rho}f(z)(z-a)^{k-1}\,dz\right| \le M\rho^k. Let \rho\downarrow0. Every negative coefficient vanishes, leaving a Taylor series. Example: \frac{\sin z}{z}=1-\frac{z^2}{3!}+\frac{z^4}{5!}-\cdots extends with value 1 at 0. Boundary: boundedness along one path is insufficient. The essential singularity e^{1/z} tends to 0 along the negative real axis but is unbounded along the positive real axis. Links: Isolated singularities · Laurent series · Cauchy estimates · Essential singularities · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 53 · 132 notes, p. 54 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Residue
text: Residue at an isolated singularity If f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n(z-a)^n on a punctured disk, then \operatorname{Res}(f,a)=c_{-1} =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|z-a|=r}f(z)\,dz, for a sufficiently small counterclockwise circle. The residue is defined for removable, pole and essential isolated singularities. Only the coefficient of power -1 contributes to the circle integral. Simple pole: \operatorname{Res}(f,a)=\lim_{z\to a}(z-a)f(z). If g,h are holomorphic near a, with h(a)=0 and h'(a)\ne0, then \operatorname{Res}(g/h,a)=\frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}. When g(a)=0, the quotient is removable and this residue is 0. Pole of order m: let G(z)=(z-a)^m f(z) extend holomorphically. Then \operatorname{Res}(f,a)=\frac{G^{(m-1)}(a)}{(m-1)!}. This extracts the Taylor coefficient of G that becomes power -1 after division by (z-a)^m. Examples: \operatorname{Res}(1/z^2,0)=0 but \operatorname{Res}(e^{1/z},0)=1. For real t, \operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{e^{itz}}{1+z^2},i\right)=\frac{e^{-t}}{2i}. Boundary: the simple-pole limit formula is not a general formula for essential singularities; use the Laurent coefficient when no finite pole order applies. Links: Laurent series · Poles and meromorphic functions · Essential singularities · Residue theorem · Cauchy integral formula · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 54 · 132 notes, p. 55 · 132 notes, p. 56 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Residue theorem
text: Residue theorem for a region Let D be a bounded region whose boundary is a finite union of disjoint piecewise C^1 simple closed curves. Suppose f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of \overline D except for finitely many isolated singularities a_1,\ldots,a_N inside D. Then \int_{\partial D}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{Res}(f,a_j). Use the full positive boundary: the region stays to the left. Singularities may be poles or essential singularities; there must be none on the integration boundary. Proof: remove small disjoint closed disks around the singularities. The function is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the remaining region. Cauchy's theorem gives \int_{\partial D}f\,dz =\sum_{j=1}^{N}\int_{|z-a_j|=r_j}f(z)\,dz, where the small circles on the right are counterclockwise. Each circle integral equals 2\pi i times its residue. Example: for a counterclockwise unit circle, \int_{|z|=1}e^{1/z}\,dz=2\pi i, even though 0 is essential rather than a pole. Boundary: the displayed formula is for the full boundary of a region. A path traversed twice gives twice the integral, and reversing it changes the sign; arbitrary closed paths require corresponding winding-number weights. A pole on the contour cannot be included by direct substitution into this theorem. Links: Residue · Cauchy's theorem · Contour integrals · Real integrals by residues · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 55 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Riemann integral
text: Let a<b be finite and f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R bounded. For a partition P:a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b, put L(f,P)=\sum_{j=1}^m\left(\inf_{[x_{j-1},x_j]}f\right)(x_j-x_{j-1}), U(f,P)=\sum_{j=1}^m\left(\sup_{[x_{j-1},x_j]}f\right)(x_j-x_{j-1}). Definition and criterion f\text{ Riemann integrable}\iff\sup_PL(f,P)=\inf_PU(f,P)=:\int_a^bf. Equivalently, \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists P:\ U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon. Sufficient conditions: continuous or monotone on [a,b] implies Riemann integrable. Products and absolute values of Riemann-integrable functions are integrable. Basic estimate: \left|\int_a^bf\right|\le\int_a^b|f|\le(b-a)\|f\|_\infty. Cauchy–Schwarz: for Riemann-integrable real or complex f,g, \int_a^b|fg|\le\left(\int_a^b|f|^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int_a^b|g|^2\right)^{1/2}. For complex functions, integrability means integrability of real and imaginary parts. The absolute squares are necessary in the complex form used in L2 space. Links: Continuity · Fundamental Theorem of Calculus · L2 space · Uniform convergence theorems · 131B · Cauchy-Schwarz inequality · Contour integrals · Real integrals by residues Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Riemann sphere
text: Extended complex plane \widehat{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}. Neighborhoods of \infty contain \{z:|z|R\}\cup\{\infty\} for some R0. Stereographic projection identifies this space with the unit sphere in \mathbb R^3. The inverse image of z=x+iy is \left(\frac{2x}{1+|z|^2},\frac{2y}{1+|z|^2},\frac{|z|^2-1}{1+|z|^2}\right). The north pole (0,0,1) corresponds to \infty; in the other direction, z=\frac{X+iY}{1-Z}\qquad(Z\ne1). As |z|\to\infty, the displayed point tends to the north pole. The coordinate w=1/z, with w=0 at \infty, turns a neighborhood of infinity into a neighborhood of 0. Notation: use \widehat{\mathbb C} for the sphere and \mathbb C\setminus\{0\} for the punctured plane. They are different spaces. The symbol \infty is an added point, not a complex number on which ordinary field arithmetic always applies. Links: Complex numbers and polar form · Möbius transformations · Holomorphic functions at infinity · Compact set · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 3 · 132 notes, p. 4 · 132 summary, p. 1

title: Rolle's Theorem
text: Theorem Let a<b, f\in C([a,b]), and suppose f is differentiable on (a,b) with f(a)=f(b). Then \exists c\in(a,b):\quad f'(c)=0. Proof: by Extreme Value Theorem, f attains max and min. If f is constant, any c\in(a,b) works. Otherwise, since the endpoint values agree, at least one extremum occurs in the interior; apply Fermat's theorem. Rolle is the f(a)=f(b) special case of MVT, and supplies its standard proof. Links: MVT · Local extrema · Continuity · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 14

title: Root test
text: Theorem Put \alpha=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}\in[0,+\infty]. - \alpha<1: \sum a_n converges absolutely. - \alpha1: \sum a_n diverges. - \alpha=1: inconclusive. Proof sketch: if \alpha<q<1, eventually |a_n|\le q^n, so use Comparison test. If 1<q<\alpha, infinitely many terms satisfy |a_n|q^n and hence a_n\not\to0. At \alpha=1: \sum1/n diverges, while \sum1/n^2 converges. The Ratio test implies the corresponding root-test conclusion when ratios are defined eventually; the converse fails. See that note for an example. Links: limsup & liminf · Absolute convergence · Comparison test · Ratio test · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 9

title: Schwarz lemma
text: Schwarz lemma Let f be holomorphic on \mathbb D=\{z:|z|<1\}, with |f(z)|\le1 and f(0)=0. Then |f(z)|\le|z|,\qquad |f'(0)|\le1. If equality holds at some z\ne0, or if |f'(0)|=1, then f(z)=\lambda z with |\lambda|=1. Proof: the zero at 0 allows the holomorphic extension g(z)=\begin{cases}f(z)/z,&z\ne0,\\f'(0),&z=0.\end{cases} For |z|<r<1, the maximum modulus principle on the radius-r disk gives |g(z)|\le\max_{|w|=r}|g(w)|\le\frac1r. Let r\uparrow1 to get |g|\le1. Either equality assumption makes |g| attain its maximum at an interior point, so g\equiv\lambda. Boundary: equality |f(0)|=|0| is automatic and gives no rigidity. For example, f(z)=z^2 satisfies the hypotheses but is not a rotation. Disk Möbius maps move a chosen point to 0, making this normalized theorem useful for other base points. Links: Maximum modulus principle · Zeros of holomorphic functions · Möbius transformations · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 42 · 132 notes, p. 43 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Spaces of functions
text: For a finite interval [a,b] with a<b, consider real-valued functions: | Space | Meaning | |---|---| | B([a,b]) | Bounded functions | | R([a,b]) | Riemann-integrable functions | | C([a,b]) | Continuous functions | | C^1([a,b]) | Continuous functions, differentiable on (a,b), with derivative extending continuously to [a,b] | C^1([a,b])\subset C([a,b])\subset R([a,b])\subset B([a,b]). Sup metric: d_\infty(f,g)=\|f-g\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in[a,b]}|f(x)-g(x)|. Convergence in this metric is exactly Uniform convergence within these spaces. Completeness: B([a,b]) is complete. C([a,b]) and R([a,b]) are closed subspaces under d_\infty because their properties survive uniform limits, so they are also complete. Caution: C^1([a,b]) with only the sup metric is not complete. On [-1,1], f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1/n}\rightrightarrows |x|,\qquad 0\le f_n(x)-|x|\le n^{-1/2}, but |x|\notin C^1([-1,1]). The metric matters; the stronger norm \|f\|_\infty+\|f'\|_\infty gives a different completeness statement. Links: Uniform convergence · Completeness of a metric space · Continuity · Riemann integral · Uniform convergence theorems · 131B · Vector space · Subspace · Linear map Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Span and linear independence
text: For S\subseteq V, \operatorname{span}S=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^ma_jv_j:m\ge0,\ a_j\in\mathbb F,\ v_j\in S\right\}. Only finite linear combinations are used, even when S is infinite. In particular, \operatorname{span}\varnothing=\{0\}. Linear independence A finite list (v_1,\ldots,v_m) is independent if \sum_{j=1}^ma_jv_j=0\implies a_1=\cdots=a_m=0. It is dependent if a nontrivial choice of coefficients gives 0. An arbitrary set is independent when every finite subset is independent. A list containing 0, or containing a repeated vector, is dependent. Useful test: a dependent list has a vector in the span of the others. Solve a nontrivial relation for a vector whose coefficient is nonzero. Independence gives uniqueness of coefficients; spanning gives existence. Together they give a basis. Function example: 1,x,\ldots,x^m are independent as real-valued functions on \mathbb R, because a polynomial that vanishes everywhere has all coefficients zero. Links: Subspace · Basis and dimension · Cyclic subspace · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 3 · 115A PDF, p. 4

title: Spectral theorem
text: Finite-dimensional spectral theorem Over \mathbb C, an operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis iff it is normal. Over \mathbb R, an operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis iff it is self-adjoint. In matrix form: A\in M_n(\mathbb C),\quad AA^=A^A \iff A=UDU^,\quad U^U=I, with D diagonal. If A is Hermitian, all entries of D are real. A\in M_n(\mathbb R),\quad A=A^{\mathsf T} \iff A=QDQ^{\mathsf T},\quad Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I, with D real diagonal. Proof route: over \mathbb C, choose an eigenvector. For a normal operator it is also an eigenvector of the adjoint, so its orthogonal complement is invariant under both T and T^. The restriction is normal; induct on dimension. For real self-adjoint operators, complexification has real eigenvalues and yields a real eigenvector, after which the same induction applies. Equivalently, for a normal complex operator (or self-adjoint real operator), T=\sum_{\lambda}\lambda P_{E_\lambda},\qquad I=\sum_{\lambda}P_{E_\lambda}, where the eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Boundary: a real rotation can be normal without real diagonalization. General diagonalizability need not allow an orthonormal eigenbasis. Links: Normal and self-adjoint operators · Orthonormal basis · Orthogonal projection · Quadratic form · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 15 · 115B PDF, p. 1

title: Subsequence
text: Definition Choose n_1<n_2<\cdots in \mathbb N. Then (x_{n_k}) is a subsequence of (x_n). - If x_n\to x, every subsequence converges to x. ^fact-subseq-limit - Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence: infinitely many peaks give a nonincreasing subsequence; after the last peak, repeatedly choose a later larger term. Here a peak is n such that x_n\ge x_m for all mn. Subsequential limits \mathcal S(x_n)=\{t\in\mathbb R:x_{n_k}\to t\text{ for some subsequence}\}. For a bounded real sequence: x_n\to L\iff\mathcal S(x_n)=\{L\}, \min\mathcal S=\liminf x_n,\qquad\max\mathcal S=\limsup x_n. Why boundedness matters: x_{2n}=0,\qquad x_{2n-1}=n. Then \mathcal S=\{0\}, but (x_n) diverges and \limsup x_n=+\infty. Proof of the singleton criterion: if x_n\not\to L, some subsequence stays at distance \ge\varepsilon from L. Boundedness and Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem give a convergent subsubsequence whose limit is not L, a contradiction. Links: Convergence of a sequence · Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem · limsup & liminf · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 3 · 131A PDF, p. 4

title: Subspace
text: Let V be a vector space over \mathbb F. Subspace test A subset W\subseteq V is a subspace if 0\in W,\qquad au+bv\in W\quad(u,v\in W,\ a,b\in\mathbb F). The operations are inherited from V; the remaining vector-space axioms need not be checked again. Examples: a homogeneous solution set \{x:Ax=0\}, polynomials of degree at most m (including 0), and continuous functions on a fixed interval. Counterexample: \{(x,y):x+y=1\} is an affine line, not a subspace: it does not contain 0. Intersections of subspaces are subspaces. A union U\cup W is a subspace iff one of U,W contains the other. The two coordinate axes in \mathbb R^2 show what can fail under addition. The smallest subspace containing a set S is its span. Links: Vector space · Kernel and image · Direct sum · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 1

title: Sup & inf
text: Let \varnothing\ne A\subseteq\mathbb R. Definition s=\sup A means \forall a\in A:\ a\le s,\qquad (\forall a\in A:\ a\le u)\implies s\le u. t=\inf A means \forall a\in A:\ t\le a,\qquad (\forall a\in A:\ \ell\le a)\implies\ell\le t. Existence in \mathbb R: bounded above \implies finite \sup A; bounded below \implies finite \inf A. This is the least-upper-bound form of completeness. Epsilon characterization s=\sup A\iff \begin{cases} a\le s&\forall a\in A,\\ \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists a\in A:\ s-\varepsilon<a. \end{cases} Example: A=(0,1) has \inf A=0, \sup A=1, but no minimum or maximum. Sup/inf need not belong to A. Links: Dedekind cut · Completeness Axiom · limsup & liminf · 131A Source: 131A PDF, p. 1

title: Sylvester law of inertia
text: Let A be a real symmetric n\times n matrix. Its inertia is (n_+,n_-,n_0), the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity. The source calls this triple the signature; some texts instead use n_+-n_- for that word. Sylvester's law of inertia For every invertible real P, A and P^{\mathsf T}AP have the same inertia. First use the Spectral theorem to diagonalize A orthogonally. Rescale the coordinates with nonzero coefficients to obtain P^{\mathsf T}AP=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_+},-I_{n_-},0_{n_0}). Why the counts are intrinsic: n_+ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax is positive definite. A subspace of larger dimension intersects the span of the nonpositive eigendirections, a contradiction. The analogous argument gives n_-; rank or nullity determines n_0. Invertible coordinate changes preserve these dimensions. Consequently, two real symmetric forms are congruent iff their inertia triples agree. Congruence preserves rank and signs, but generally not individual eigenvalues: \operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{diag}(4,-9) are congruent. Similarity instead describes a change of coordinates for an operator and preserves its individual eigenvalues. Links: Quadratic form · Positive definite matrix · Spectral theorem · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Quadratic form

title: Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions
text: Holomorphic implies analytic If f is holomorphic on D(a,R), then f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(z-a)^n \qquad(|z-a|<R). The series has radius at least R and converges uniformly on every smaller closed disk. For 0<r<R, its coefficients are a_n=\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|w-a|=r}\frac{f(w)}{(w-a)^{n+1}}\,dw. Proof idea: for |z-a|<r, expand the Cauchy kernel as a geometric series: \frac1{w-z}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z-a)^n}{(w-a)^{n+1}} \qquad(|w-a|=r). The series is uniform on this fixed contour, so integrate term by term. Cauchy estimates give uniform convergence on smaller disks; let r range below R. Examples: \frac1{1-z}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n\quad(|z|<1),\qquad e^z=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{n!}\quad(z\in\mathbb C), \operatorname{Log}(1+z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}n z^n\quad(|z|<1). The last identity uses the branch with \operatorname{Log}(1)=0. Boundary: unlike a merely smooth real function, a holomorphic function cannot have all derivatives zero at an interior point without being zero nearby. The coefficients are unique; the given domain need not be the maximal domain of convergence. Links: Taylor series · Complex power series · Cauchy integral formula · Cauchy estimates · Zeros of holomorphic functions · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 35 · 132 notes, p. 41 · 132 notes, p. 42 · 132 notes, p. 43 · 132 notes, p. 44 · 132 summary, p. 1 · 132 summary, p. 2

title: Taylor series
text: For f smooth on a neighborhood of c, its Taylor series at c is \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(c)}{n!}(x-c)^n. Forming this series does not assert convergence or equality with f. First-order approximation Differentiability at x gives f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)h+o(|h|). The stronger remainder O(h^2) follows, for example, when f\in C^2 near x (by the Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder). It does not follow from differentiability alone: f(h)=|h|^{3/2} at 0. Analytic versus smooth f is analytic at c if it equals a convergent power series on a neighborhood of c. Its coefficients then equal f^{(n)}(c)/n!. Smooth does not imply analytic f(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-1/|x|},&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0.\end{cases} This function is C^\infty, all derivatives at 0 vanish, but f(x)0 for x\ne0. Its Taylor series at 0 is identically 0. Reason: every derivative away from 0 is an exponential times a polynomial in 1/|x| (with side-dependent signs); t^m e^{-t}\to0 as t\to\infty for every m. This also controls the difference quotients at 0. Example: e^x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n/n!, with radius +\infty. Links: Power series · Derivative · Generalized MVT · 131B · Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Uniform continuity
text: Let f:(X,d_X)\to(Y,d_Y) be a map between metric spaces. Definition \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists\delta0\ \forall x,y\in X: d_X(x,y)<\delta\implies d_Y(f(x),f(y))<\varepsilon. One \delta=\delta(\varepsilon) works everywhere. For ordinary continuity, \delta may also depend on the base point. \text{Lipschitz}\implies\text{uniformly continuous}\implies\text{continuous}. Heine–Cantor A continuous map from a compact metric space to a metric space is uniformly continuous. Proof by contradiction: if not, choose x_n,y_n with d_X(x_n,y_n)<1/n,\qquad d_Y(f(x_n),f(y_n))\ge\varepsilon_0. Compactness gives x_{n_k}\to x\in X, hence y_{n_k}\to x. Continuity and the triangle inequality contradict the lower bound. Consequences and their hypotheses - Uniformly continuous maps send Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences, whether or not a limit lies in the domain. - If E\subseteq\mathbb R^d is bounded and f:E\to\mathbb R uniformly continuous, then f is bounded. Reason: cover E by finitely many balls at the \delta-scale for \varepsilon=1. - For finite a<b, f:(a,b)\to\mathbb R has a continuous extension to [a,b] iff f is uniformly continuous. Define endpoint values by limits of Cauchy images; completeness of \mathbb R gives existence, uniform continuity gives independence of the approaching sequence. The extension is unique and uniformly continuous. General metric caution: bounded domain alone is insufficient for bounded image. On \mathbb N with discrete metric d(m,n)=1 for m\ne n, f(n)=n is uniformly continuous but unbounded. The finite-cover argument needs total boundedness (a finite \delta-net for every \delta0). Strict implications: \sqrt{x} on [0,1] is uniformly continuous but not Lipschitz; 1/x on (0,1) is continuous but not uniformly continuous. Links: Continuity · Compact set · Cauchy sequence · Compactness and continuity · 131A · 131B Source: 131A PDF, p. 12 · 131A PDF, p. 13

title: Uniform convergence
text: Definition For real-valued functions on S, f_n\rightrightarrows f\iff \forall\varepsilon0\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N\ \forall x\in S: |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon. For nonempty S, equivalently \sup_{x\in S}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0. On bounded-function spaces, this is convergence in the sup metric. Uniform convergence can also be considered for unbounded functions, provided their differences satisfy the displayed condition. Uniform \implies pointwise; the converse fails for x^n on [0,1]. Uniform convergence preserves continuity Theorem On a metric domain S, if every f_n is continuous and f_n\rightrightarrows f, then f is continuous. Proof: fix x_0\in S, \varepsilon0. First choose one n with \sup_S|f_n-f|<\varepsilon/3. Then continuity of this f_n gives \delta0 such that d(x,x_0)<\delta implies |f(x)-f(x_0)|\le |f(x)-f_n(x)|+|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|+|f_n(x_0)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon. The order is choose n, then choose \delta. More preservation results: Uniform convergence theorems. Links: Continuity · Pointwise convergence · Spaces of functions · 131A · 131B · Locally uniform convergence Source: 131A PDF, p. 15

title: Uniform convergence theorems
text: All functions below are real-valued; \rightrightarrows means uniform convergence on the stated common domain. Continuity preservation is proved in Uniform convergence. Boundedness and uniform continuity - Bounded f_n, f_n\rightrightarrows f \implies f bounded: choose one n with \|f-f_n\|_\infty<1. - Uniformly continuous f_n on a metric space, f_n\rightrightarrows f \implies f uniformly continuous: choose one n for two \varepsilon/3 approximation errors, then use its uniform continuity for the middle term. Integration on a finite interval If each f_n is Riemann integrable on [a,b], a<b finite, and f_n\rightrightarrows f, then f is Riemann integrable and \left|\int_a^bf_n-\int_a^bf\right|\le(b-a)\|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0. For integrability, compare Darboux sums: U(f,P)-L(f,P)\le U(f_n,P)-L(f_n,P)+2(b-a)\|f-f_n\|_\infty. Choose n first, then P. Differentiation A sufficient theorem Let f_n\in C^1([a,b]), a<b finite. If f_n'\rightrightarrows g and f_n(x_0)\to\ell for one x_0\in[a,b], then f_n\rightrightarrows f, where f(x)=\ell+\int_{x_0}^xg(t)\,dt,\qquad f'=g\text{ on }(a,b). Proof: g is continuous by uniform convergence, and FTC gives \|f_n-f\|_\infty\le|f_n(x_0)-\ell|+(b-a)\|f_n'-g\|_\infty\to0. Why the assumptions matter - f_n\rightrightarrows f alone need not preserve differentiability: \sqrt{x^2+1/n}\rightrightarrows |x| on [-1,1]. - Without convergence at one point, constants f_n=n have f_n'=0 but no function limit. - On an unbounded interval, global uniform convergence of f_n need not follow: f_n(x)=x/n on \mathbb R has f_n'\rightrightarrows0 and f_n(0)=0, but f_n does not converge uniformly. The corresponding conclusion is uniform convergence on each compact interval. Links: Uniform convergence · Pointwise convergence · Uniform continuity · Riemann integral · Derivative · Weierstrass M-test · 131B · Locally uniform convergence Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Unitary and orthogonal operators
text: Let U be an operator on a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Unitary / orthogonal Over \mathbb C, U is unitary if U^U=UU^=I. Over \mathbb R, the corresponding term is orthogonal. The following are equivalent in finite dimension: U^U=I,\qquad U^{-1}=U^,\qquad \langle Ux,Uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle\quad(x,y\in V). They are also equivalent to preservation of every norm \|Ux\|=\|x\|, by polarization. Norm preservation gives injectivity; finite dimension gives surjectivity. In orthonormal coordinates, the columns of a unitary matrix form an orthonormal basis. A unitary operator is normal; every eigenvalue has modulus 1, since \|\lambda x\|=\|x\|. For a real orthogonal matrix Q, Q^{-1}=Q^{\mathsf T} and \det Q=\pm1. The determinant alone is not a test for orthogonality. Examples: plane rotations have determinant 1; reflection across a line has determinant -1. A rotation through an angle other than 0 or \pi has no real eigenvectors, despite preserving lengths. Unitary similarity B=U^AU preserves the inner product as well as the operator's algebraic structure. General similarity need not preserve lengths or angles. Links: Adjoint · Orthonormal basis · Normal and self-adjoint operators · Spectral theorem · 115B Source: 115B PDF, p. 1 · 原图区域：Spectral thm

title: Vector space
text: Let \mathbb F be a field. The course mainly uses \mathbb R and \mathbb C. Definition A vector space over \mathbb F is a set V with addition and scalar multiplication such that (V,+) is an abelian group and, for a,b\in\mathbb F and u,v\in V, a(u+v)=au+av,\quad(a+b)v=av+bv, a(bv)=(ab)v,\qquad1v=v. The operations take values in V. The zero vector belongs to V; 0v=0_V and (-1)v=-v follow from the axioms. Examples: \mathbb F^n, matrices of a fixed size, polynomials, and functions X\to\mathbb F with pointwise operations: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x),\qquad(af)(x)=af(x). The scalar field matters: \mathbb C has dimension 1 over \mathbb C and dimension 2 over \mathbb R. A vector need not be an arrow; functions are vectors too. Field reminder: 0\ne1, and every nonzero scalar has a multiplicative inverse. This qualification is needed in the source's list of field axioms. Links: Subspace · Basis and dimension · Spaces of functions · 115A Source: 115A PDF, p. 1 · 115A PDF, p. 2

title: Weierstrass Approximation Theorem
text: Theorem Let a<b be finite. For f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R) and every \varepsilon0, there is an ordinary real polynomial P such that \sup_{x\in[a,b]}|f(x)-P(x)|<\varepsilon. Polynomials are dense in C([a,b]) under the sup norm. Landau-kernel proof map The source board sketches convolution and polynomial approximation. The following makes the endpoint extension and domain restrictions explicit. 1. Rescale to I=[-1/2,1/2]. Subtract the linear interpolant \ell of f at the endpoints. Then g=f-\ell vanishes at both endpoints, so extending g by 0 outside I gives a continuous compactly supported function. 2. Set K_n(t)=c_n(1-t^2)^n\mathbf1_{[-1,1]}(t),\qquad c_n^{-1}=\int_{-1}^1(1-t^2)^n\,dt\quad(n\ge1). These nonnegative kernels have mass 1 and concentrate at 0. For 0<\eta<1, \int_{|t|\ge\eta}K_n(t)\,dt \le\frac2\eta\left(\frac{1-\eta^2}{1-\eta^2/4}\right)^n\to0. 3. For x\in I, every y\in I has |x-y|\le1, so (gK_n)(x)=c_n\int_I g(y)\bigl(1-(x-y)^2\bigr)^n\,dy=:P_n(x). The last expression defines a polynomial in x (degree at most 2n). 4. By approximate identity, P_n\to g uniformly on I. Add \ell and undo the affine rescaling. The cutoff kernel is not a polynomial on all of \mathbb R; the restricted interval in step 3 is what makes the approximant polynomial. Links: Convolution · Fourier theorem · Spaces of functions · 131B Supplementary check: [A. Pinkus, Weierstrass and Approximation Theory, Landau proof, pp. 31–32](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/hat/fpapers/wap.pdfpage=31). The proof above uses a zero-endpoint extension to express the same approximation mechanism. Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Weierstrass M-test
text: Theorem Let f_n:X\to\mathbb R or \mathbb C, where X\ne\varnothing. If |f_n(x)|\le M_n\quad\forall x\in X,\qquad M_n\ge0,\qquad\sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n<\infty, then both \sum f_n and \sum|f_n| converge uniformly on X. Proof by tails: for mn, \sup_{x\in X}\left|\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}f_k(x)\right| \le\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}M_k\le\sum_{kn}M_k\to0. The partial sums are sup-Cauchy; use completeness of bounded functions. The same bound applies to the series of absolute values. Convenient form: \sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty is sufficient for uniform convergence. Not necessary: constant functions f_n(x)=(-1)^n/n form a uniformly convergent series (its numerical tails are independent of x), but \sum\|f_n\|_\infty=\infty. Links: Uniform convergence theorems · Absolute convergence · Comparison test · Power series · 131B Source: 131B PDF, p. 1

title: Zeros of holomorphic functions
text: Let f be holomorphic near a, with f(a)=0, and not identically zero near a. Order of a zero The order is the smallest m\ge1 for which f^{(m)}(a)\ne0. Equivalently, f(z)=(z-a)^m h(z), where h is holomorphic near a and h(a)\ne0. Use the first nonzero coefficient in the Taylor series. Continuity keeps h nonzero on a smaller disk, so a is an isolated zero. The orders of zeros add under multiplication. Isolated zeros theorem: if f is holomorphic and not identically zero on a domain D, every zero in D has finite order and is isolated. To justify finite order, consider the set where all derivatives vanish. Taylor expansion makes this set open, while continuity of every derivative makes it closed. Connectedness forces it to be empty unless f\equiv0. Useful division: if f(0)=0, then f(z)/z extends holomorphically at 0, with value f'(0). This is the step used in Schwarz's lemma. Boundary: isolated does not mean finitely many zeros on the whole domain; \sin z has infinitely many. On any compact subset of D, however, a nonzero holomorphic function has only finitely many zeros, since an infinite set would have a limit point inside D. Links: Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions · Identity theorem · Schwarz lemma · Poles and meromorphic functions · Connectedness · 132 Source: 132 notes, p. 42 · 132 notes, p. 43 · 132 notes, p. 45 · 132 notes, p. 46 · 132 summary, p. 2
